taches.questions:
Understanding how the human brain transforms visual stimuli into structured patterns of neural activity remains one of the fundamental challenges in computational neuroscience. This task, commonly referred to as brain visual encoding, seeks to model the functional mapping from external visual perception to spatially distributed neural responses across the cortex, uncovering how high-level visual semantics are represented in neural populations. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has emerged as a dominant modality for brain encoding: as a noninvasive neuroimaging technique, it measures blood-oxygen-level-dependent signals as indirect proxies for neuronal activity with high spatial resolution. By translating visual inputs into fMRI-measured neural patterns, brain encoding models not only advance our understanding of human visual perception but also lay the groundwork for applications in neural decoding, cognitive modeling, and brain-machine interfaces.

Recent advances in brain encoding have predominantly adopted either regression-based or deterministic generative strategies to map visual stimuli or their semantic representations to the corresponding fMRI recordings. Regression models typically learn a deterministic function that directly predicts voxel-level brain activity from visual stimuli using linear regression or deep neural networks. Generative brain encoding methods such as MindSimulator instead reformulate brain encoding as a visual-to-fMRI synthesis process conditioned on visual input: MindSimulator uses a deterministic MLP-based autoencoder to reconstruct brain activity from semantic features and aligns the fMRI latent space to visual stimuli via a diffusion-based semantic-to-latent mapping. Its stochasticity is introduced only at inference time, via diffusion sampling started from Gaussian noise, and it relies on averaging multiple samples and heuristic post-selection to produce stable and plausible outputs.

However, such deterministic strategies fail to model the inherent one-to-many nature of neural signals. Large-scale neuroimaging studies indicate that repeated presentations of the same visual stimulus can elicit notably different fMRI responses across trials and subjects. This highlights a fundamental characteristic of brain activity: the mapping from visual stimuli to neural responses is inherently one-to-many, influenced by trial-level noise, attentional fluctuations, and inter-individual variability. At the same time, neural responses exhibit variability while maintaining consistent function: the specific patterns vary, yet the encoding of stimulus information remains consistent.

Given this property, existing methods face three key limitations. (1) Deterministic neural modeling: deterministic models produce a unique latent representation per input and often collapse diverse neural patterns into a non-informative averaged response that lacks semantic or physiological validity; even when variability is introduced through stochastic sampling, the core fMRI synthesis module may remain deterministic. (2) Lack of functionally-consistent variability: current approaches fail to model neural responses that are simultaneously variable in their specific patterns yet consistent in their functional encoding of stimulus information. (3) Limited utility as synthetic training data: collecting high-quality fMRI data is expensive, time-consuming, and subject to strong individual variability, so decoding models for new individuals often must make do with very little data; yet the lack of cross-subject transferability of existing encoding models restricts their applicability as augmentation sources for neural decoding in such data-limited scenarios.

These challenges motivate a key research question: how can we effectively model the distribution of neural responses to visual stimuli while preserving functional consistency? Related questions follow: can such a model synthesize fMRI signals that are faithful at the voxel level and semantically consistent with the stimulus, can it adapt to new subjects from limited data, and can the signals it synthesizes serve as useful training data for decoding visual stimuli from brain activity when real recordings are scarce?

taches.questions:
Positional information is essential for sequence modeling with Transformers, whose self-attention is otherwise permutation-invariant. Early work injected absolute positional codes (sinusoidal or learned) into token representations. Later, relative encodings depending on offsets and linear logit biases such as ALiBi were introduced, the latter offering strong length extrapolation with negligible overhead. Forgetting mechanisms such as the Forgetting Transformer (FoX) add data-dependent, cumulative decay terms to the attention logits.

Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) realizes relative positions as orthogonal planar rotations of queries and keys, preserving norms and yielding exact origin invariance of attention scores. Despite its appeal, RoPE fixes coordinate planes and typically a log-uniform spectrum, limiting cross-subspace coupling and contextual warping of phase. More broadly, absolute codes break translation equivariance, and table-based relative encodings add window-dependent overhead. Richer rotational encodings that learn dense skew-symmetric generators exist, but applying a full matrix exponential per head is costly, especially when the generator must depend on token content.

Current methods thus isolate the essential properties of stability, monotonic distance penalty, and expressivity: multiplicative rotary schemes and additive or forgetting bias schemes are treated as separate families with different foundations. This raises several questions. Is there a single formulation that (i) preserves RoPE's orthogonality and exact relativity when desired, (ii) also covers additive and forgetting mechanisms such as ALiBi and FoX, and (iii) admits learned and contextual generalizations while keeping clean streaming, so that keys can be cached once at inference? Can such generalizations capture cross-subspace coupling at modest computational cost? And would positional encodings designed within such a formulation bring practical benefits to language models?

taches.questions:
Accurate and timely short-term precipitation forecasts, or nowcasting, are of paramount importance due to their significant socio-economic impacts, such as issuing flood warnings and managing water resources. Precipitation nowcasting involves predicting a sequence of future radar images from historical observations for the immediate future, up to a few hours. Traditional methods, like Eulerian and Lagrangian persistence, rely on advecting the current precipitation field. However, their simplified physical assumptions limit their ability to capture the complex, non-linear dynamics of atmospheric processes, especially for rapidly evolving weather systems.

Deep learning has introduced a paradigm shift in precipitation nowcasting. Deterministic models based on recurrent and transformer architectures (e.g., ConvLSTM, the PredRNN family, Earthformer, Earthfarseer) learn complex spatiotemporal patterns directly from large volumes of radar data. While these models outperform traditional methods, optimizing for metrics like Mean Squared Error compels them to produce a single, best-guess forecast. Because they average over possible futures, this often results in overly smooth predictions at longer lead times, failing to capture the inherent uncertainty in precipitation evolution and underrepresenting high-impact weather events.

To address this, probabilistic generative models have become central to modern nowcasting, aiming to predict a distribution over many plausible futures. GANs were an early approach for producing sharp forecasts but suffer from training instability. Diffusion models have since emerged as the state of the art, producing sharp and reliable ensemble forecasts; prominent examples include latent diffusion models for ensemble forecasting and hybrids that use a deterministic model for large-scale patterns and a conditional diffusion model to refine stochastic details. However, their reliance on an iterative denoising process, often requiring hundreds of function evaluations for a single forecast, makes them computationally expensive. This high number of function evaluations poses a significant barrier in time-critical scenarios where rapid ensemble generation is crucial. Classical continuous normalizing flows, another family of generative models, require expensive numerical integration during training to compute likelihoods, making them computationally prohibitive for high-dimensional spatiotemporal data.

Two challenges therefore remain fundamental: representing the uncertainty of atmospheric dynamics and efficiently modeling high-dimensional radar data. The open question is whether a probabilistic nowcasting model can produce sharp, well-calibrated ensemble forecasts that capture extreme precipitation, at a level matching or exceeding leading diffusion models and deterministic baselines, while requiring far fewer function evaluations at inference time, so as to ease the tension between forecast accuracy and computational efficiency in operational settings.

taches.questions:
Prediction and modeling of time series data is ubiquitous in data analysis, with applications across a broad range of fields including climate science, energy forecasting, healthcare, consumer behavior modeling, and financial forecasting. Traditional statistical approaches such as linear autoregressive (AR) models and associated variants are well-established in the field; they have been supplemented in recent years by a variety of machine learning approaches using richer model representations, including deep learning time series models such as N-BEATS and Informer.

A more recent trend is the emergence of time series foundation models (TSFMs). Unlike traditional statistical and machine learning approaches where models are fitted to time series from a single source, TSFMs are general-purpose models trained on a broad range of time series from various domains and are capable of zero-shot or few-shot forecasting on any time series in principle. This is appealing to practitioners in that only a single global model is required rather than retraining a new model for every time series.

With this increase of interest in TSFMs, it becomes important to understand and characterize the calibration properties of such models. TSFMs, in general, produce conditional distributions over potential future values, rather than just single point forecasts. This distributional information is important and useful in many applications. In particular, it can be essential for decision-making, for example in downstream tasks such as anomaly detection and in critical domains such as healthcare. A natural question in this context is: how well calibrated are TSFMs in terms of their conditional distributions, i.e., how well do the predicted probabilities match the observed data? A related question is whether they are systematically miscalibrated in one direction, since deep learning models in image classification and large language models in question answering have often been shown to be overconfident.

While the calibration properties of classification and regression models have received considerable attention in machine learning in recent years, the calibration properties of TSFMs remain relatively underexplored. Evaluations of probabilistic time series forecasters commonly rely on the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS), the Weighted Quantile Loss (WQL), and the Mean Scaled Interval Score (MSIS), and using these metrics prior works have claimed that TSFMs are better calibrated than baseline methods like ARIMA and N-BEATS. However, it has been proved that these metrics measure a combination of both probabilistic calibration and sharpness rather than calibration alone, a combination that can skew evaluation towards prioritizing predictive sharpness. Whether TSFMs are well calibrated in the strict sense therefore remains an open question.

Two design aspects of TSFMs raise further calibration questions. First, TSFMs produce conditional distributions in different ways: some models predict the parameters of conditional density models, while others predict sets of conditional quantiles, and parametric, categorical and mixture heads have all been proposed in the literature. Does the form of the prediction head affect calibration? Second, TSFMs vary in their approaches to long-term forecasting beyond the forecast horizon (the prediction length of a single forward pass). Many TSFMs rely on autoregressive forecasting, and prior works have shown that autoregressive forecasting can have negative effects on model performance due to the reinitialization of the probabilistic forecast; alternatives include multi-patch forecasting and stochastic autoregression that propagates probabilistic information to subsequent forecasts. How do limited forecast horizons and the choice of autoregressive scheme affect calibration on long-term forecasts?

taches.questions:
Personalization in text-to-image generation involves the targeted adaptation of models to learn representations of novel, user-provided concepts. This process allows for the creation of customized images that faithfully render specific concepts, such as unique individuals, objects, or artistic styles, in new contexts.

Current personalization approaches fall into two paradigms: parameter fine-tuning and embedding optimization. Parameter fine-tuning methods, exemplified by DreamBooth, optimize entire models using a few user-provided images. While effective, these approaches are computationally expensive and require significant storage per concept. In contrast, embedding optimization methods, such as Textual Inversion (TI), offer a more efficient alternative by optimizing only token embeddings. This approach provides substantial advantages: minimal storage per concept and seamless workflow integration. These advantages have made TI a foundational component in numerous personalization frameworks, and align with a broader paradigm shared with other domains, such as prompt tuning in large language models and personalization of vision-language models.

Despite its utility, TI suffers from critical limitations. The fundamental challenge stems from the restrictive constraint of optimizing a single embedding vector to encapsulate highly complex and multifaceted visual concepts. This limitation leads to two key problems. First, TI struggles to maintain high fidelity to complex prompts, compromising its controllability and expressive range: a prompt asking for a personalized subject in a given style, wearing an accessory, or in a particular background may render the subject but omit the other requested details. Second, the extensive fine-tuning duration required to learn each new concept hinders its practical applicability for rapid, user-driven workflows. Recent works have attempted to address these limitations through enriched embedding spaces, but introduce significant computational overhead that undermines TI's efficiency advantage. Moreover, these existing methods treat the symptoms rather than directly addressing the underlying optimization dynamics of TI, leaving the fundamental geometric factors that govern semantic alignment in embedding-based personalization largely unclear.

This raises several questions. What happens to a learned token embedding during TI optimization, and how does it come to differ from the embeddings of the pre-trained vocabulary? Which geometric properties of the token embedding space carry semantic information, and how do the properties of a learned embedding affect the way the text encoder contextualizes the personalized token with the rest of the prompt? And can embedding-only personalization be made faithful to complex prompts while preserving the subject's identity and keeping TI's lightweight cost and storage profile?

taches.questions:
Despite their remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, the inner workings of Large Language Models (LLMs) remain poorly understood. This lack of transparency is particularly problematic in high-stakes scenarios, where LLMs are prone to hallucinations: cases in which the model generates false or fabricated content. Accurate hallucination detection is critical for the safe and reliable deployment of LLMs. Existing detection methods often rely on auxiliary LLMs or repeated prompting, but these approaches tend to be slow and computationally intensive, taking up to several seconds per instance. A prominent class of methods avoids this cost through probing classifiers: simple models, often linear, trained on internal LLM representations to predict certain attributes. Probing has been central to interpretability research and is increasingly used as a predictive or control tool, yet most hallucination and error detectors still probe a single token (often the final answer token or the final prompt token) at a single layer.

Traditional probing classifiers have two fundamental limitations. First, they operate on isolated layer-token pairs, neglecting information carried by the rest of the model's activations. While predictive hallucination signals may appear at specific "exact tokens", their positions vary across responses, so locating them is a difficult problem in its own right, in practice requiring additional (possibly multiple) LLM queries; these signals may also peak at different layers depending on the dataset. Whether the most informative positions also differ across LLMs on the same task is an open question, and if they do, any fixed probing location is unlikely to transfer between models. Second, probing classifiers are model-specific: they cannot generalize across LLMs or benefit from hallucination-related information found in other LLMs. This hinders sharing datasets across LLMs, transfer learning, and multi-model training. Crucially, each new LLM or text generation task demands annotating a new dataset, which is tricky and sometimes impractical.

Using the full internal state of an LLM for a response, all layers across all generated tokens, is appealing but challenging: it is large, high-dimensional, and its shape (number of layers, hidden dimension, response length) differs across LLMs and inputs. For instance, a transformer with 50 layers, 512 tokens and 4096 hidden dimensions produces about 0.2GB of activations per response in float16. Moreover, the hidden representations of different LLMs are not directly comparable, since even functionally identical networks can produce feature spaces that differ by internal symmetries such as neuron permutations; recent work on representation alignment nonetheless suggests that different LLMs may converge towards a shared, approximately linearly related representation of reality, including of factual truth.

In a white-box setting with full access to the LLM's internal states, but without external resources such as search engines or auxiliary LLMs, and restricted to a single generation pass, we therefore ask: (i) Can a detector be designed that processes the full internal state of an LLM and benefits from it, while remaining efficient enough for real-world deployment? (ii) Can such a detector learn across multiple LLMs and benefit from it? Beyond the standard in-domain setting, where annotated data are available for the target LLM and task, two more challenging scenarios are of interest: generalizing to tasks or domains not seen during training for a known LLM, and generalizing to a previously unseen LLM when little or no annotated data are available for it.

taches.questions:
Video generation has emerged as a transformative technology, powering applications in gaming, animation, autonomous driving, digital avatars and robotics. Modern video generative models can produce photo-realistic videos from text or single images. However, they often lack physical plausibility, controllability over dynamic physical behaviors and high fidelity, because they are trained on massive 2D videos in a purely data-driven manner. Prior work has shown that additional control signals, such as camera movement, human pose or point movement, can be injected into pretrained video models, but these models lack an understanding of physical laws, often generate physically implausible outputs, and cannot support explicit physics control such as specifying material properties or applied forces.

To achieve physics-grounded video generation, incorporating inductive biases of physical dynamics is crucial. Recent works have combined physics simulators with neural representations (e.g., Gaussian splats) to simulate rigid or non-rigid dynamics and render them into videos, but they operate under scene-specific settings, require high-quality 3D reconstruction, or use video models only for texture refinement. While physics simulators based on Newtonian mechanics can model the dynamics of diverse real-world systems, including soft and rigid bodies, fluids and gases, they suffer from high computational cost, sensitivity to hyperparameters (e.g., simulation substeps, grid size), numerical instabilities, and trade-offs between generality and accuracy. As a result, when a physics simulator is used directly for video generation, one has to tune several hyperparameters and might need to switch simulators depending on the object material (e.g., MPM for elastic objects and rigid-body simulators for rigid ones); such pipelines can also lack robustness and be slow, especially for inverse problems. Learned alternatives have their own limitations: physics-informed neural networks are restricted to per-scene optimization, graph neural network simulators typically rely on next-step prediction and are susceptible to drift and error accumulation over time, and existing generative models of 4D dynamics are trained on a limited number of shapes covering mainly human and animal motions.

This raises the problem of achieving physics-grounded image-to-video generation from a single image with explicit control over physical parameters (such as stiffness) and external forces, in a way that is robust, efficient and generalizable across diverse material types. Two fundamental questions arise. First, what is an appropriate representation of physical dynamics for providing control to video models, one that enables efficient control of the video model while generalizing across a wide range of materials? Second, how can generative physics priors across various materials be embedded into a network so that the dynamics it predicts are physically plausible?

taches.questions:
Anomaly detection is the basis of many critical applications, including cybersecurity, healthcare, and industrial maintenance. By enabling the identification of abnormalities, potential threats, or critical system failures, it contributes to the robustness and safety of real-world systems. Despite its significance, anomaly detection remains challenging because anomalous behaviours are hard to characterise and little prior knowledge about anomalous samples is available. Consequently, it is commonly approached as an unsupervised representation learning problem without access to labelled anomalies.

A standard approach in unsupervised anomaly detection trains a model to learn a compact representation of the normal samples in a training dataset, under the assumption that the training data is clean, i.e. contains only normal samples; anomalies are then identified as deviations from this learned normality. One-class classification methods learn a decision boundary that encompasses all normal samples, density-based methods learn the probability distribution of normal samples, and memory bank-based approaches store the features of normal samples. However, real-world datasets are often contaminated with undetected or mislabeled anomalies. For example, a dataset collected for industrial maintenance may already include unnoticed defects. As the proportion of anomalies grows, the trained model becomes biased towards anomalous regions, and its ability to distinguish normal from anomalous instances degrades.

Existing approaches to handle contamination in the unsupervised setting mainly follow two strategies: filtering out suspected anomalies with an auxiliary one-class classifier, or modifying the training pipeline to make it robust to contamination. Although effective, these methods rely on prior knowledge of the contamination ratio, which is typically unknown, and they are often computationally expensive. Estimating the contamination ratio is itself difficult: proposals either assume an auxiliary dataset with a known ratio from a similar domain, or fit mixture models to anomaly scores without a closed-form solution. In the semi-supervised setting, methods leverage additional labelled normal and anomalous samples, but their effectiveness diminishes when the anomalies seen during training do not replicate real-world anomalies.

A particularly challenging and increasingly common setting is one in which the training pipeline, the training data, and any prior knowledge of the proportion of anomalies cannot be accessed. This reflects the growing trend of deploying proprietary, pre-trained anomaly detection models, where access to internal model components is often restricted. Even when fine-tuning is permitted, it is computationally intensive and unreliable, because clean training data cannot be guaranteed when anomalies are unknown a priori. Adaptation methods that require no special preparation of the model have been studied in other areas, but remain largely unexplored in the context of anomaly detection.

The research question is therefore: given an unsupervised anomaly detection model that has already been trained on a possibly contaminated dataset, and without retraining it, accessing its training data or pipeline, or knowing the contamination ratio, how can the adverse effects of contamination on its detection performance be mitigated? Any such solution should be applicable across diverse anomaly detection model families and data modalities, should not require labelled data, and should remain reliable across different levels of contamination.

taches.questions:
Diffusion and flow matching models have achieved remarkable success in generative modeling across domains including image generation, protein design, and text generation. As intrinsically iterative processes that gradually transform random noise into meaningful samples, their inference usually requires hundreds to up to a thousand steps for decent generation. To mitigate this high computational cost, consistency models were proposed: by "shortcutting" the probability flow ordinary differential equation and enforcing consistent model outputs along it, they can generate high-quality samples in one or a few steps. A consistency model can be obtained either by distillation, where a pre-trained flow matching model approximates the marginal vector field (consistency distillation), or by training directly on the conditional vector field (consistency training), which, with a stop-gradient operation, has the same marginalization effect. On images, consistency models have surpassed earlier distillation approaches and rectified flows in one-step generation.

Beyond Euclidean domains like images, generative models on Riemannian manifolds have a potentially profound impact in scientific domains, including protein generation, peptide design, robotics, and geoscience. For example, the generative modeling of a protein requires descriptors of the position, orientation, and torsion angles of each amino acid: while the position is Euclidean, the orientation lies in the 3D rotation group SO(3) and the torsion angles lie on a flat torus, where a translation by 2π yields the same angle. Existing generative models for protein design typically require 200 to 1000 sampling steps, limiting the throughput for virtual screening. A fast and effective few-step generative model on Riemannian manifolds could therefore significantly accelerate drug discovery and enzyme design. Diffusion and flow matching models have been extended to Riemannian manifolds, yet one-step or few-step generation on Riemannian manifolds remains largely unexplored.

Extending consistency models to Riemannian manifolds poses challenges that do not arise in the Euclidean case, where the distance between two predictions is simply measured with the Euclidean norm. The intrinsically curved manifold requires the consistency parameterization (the model's prediction of the clean sample) to lie on the manifold, so the simple linear interpolation schemes used by Euclidean consistency models are not always feasible. Furthermore, the manifold constraint imposes an additional constraint on the vector field when the consistency loss is enforced: the vector field at different points must lie in the corresponding tangent spaces, which are not directly comparable, so the time derivative along the flow requires additional corrections. A consistency model on a manifold must therefore be fully aware of the intrinsic geometry to shortcut the Riemannian probability flow.

This raises several questions. How can the consistency principle be formulated on a general Riemannian manifold so that predictions remain on the manifold and consistency is measured intrinsically? What do the discrete- and continuous-time training objectives look like in this setting, and can training on conditional vector fields still substitute for distillation from a pre-trained teacher, as it does in the Euclidean case? How can such objectives be computed efficiently on manifolds whose geometric operations may be complicated? Finally, is respecting the manifold geometry actually necessary for high-quality few-step generation, or would simpler adaptations of existing Euclidean approaches suffice?

taches.questions:
Humans develop strong semantic object representations from an egocentric visual stream with only little supervision. These semantic representations reflect different non-perceptual facets of an object, such as its identity, fine-grained category, basic category, or its typical context of occurrence. Models trained with self-supervised learning (SSL) are reasonably good models of biological vision, but they are poor models of visual learning, as they rely on different training data and learning mechanisms than humans. This may be the reason why they fail to model human semantic object similarity judgments and under-perform at recognizing objects when trained on visual experience similar to that of humans.

To learn semantic representations from their natural visual experience, humans may rely on two aspects of biological vision that are typically neglected in current models. First, the stimuli received by the human visual cortex differ structurally from egocentric videos. The human retina samples information from the center of the field of view more densely, such that high-fidelity information is only available within several degrees from the center of the visual field, i.e., in central vision. As a consequence, central vision plays a crucial role in the formation of object-level representations in areas of the visual cortex related to semantic information. To compensate for the relatively low acuity in peripheral vision, humans move their gaze around three times per second to parse their environment. Second, a key principle of biological learning states that biological systems assign similar representations to close-in-time visual inputs. This may be important when learning from central visual experience. For instance, observing objects from different viewpoints may favor viewpoint-invariant object representations, and consecutive scanning of objects within the same context may support object representations that encode their context of occurrence, a feature of human semantic object perception (the presence of a knife, for example, often reflects a "kitchen" context).

Prior work leaves the combination of these two aspects largely unexplored. The increased availability of datasets collected with head-mounted cameras has induced a surge of egocentric SSL models, but these approaches use the entire high-resolution field of view captured by the camera. Methods that learn similar representations for close-in-time visual inputs have mostly been studied on synthetic data, curated visual sequences of interactions with objects, third-person videos, or videos recorded from cars, rather than on in-the-wild human egocentric experience. Studies that model the space-variant resolution of the retina, including recent ones combining it with time-based SSL, have trained with only a tiny number of objects, which leaves open the role of such bio-inspired learning for semantic recognition at scale. Finally, only few works have studied the emergence of similar representations for objects that co-occur in the same context, and it remains unclear how and whether the natural experience of humans supports the construction of object representations reflecting their typical context of appearance.

At present, it is therefore unclear how self-supervision with a slowness objective and a human-like focus on central vision may shape the semantic properties of learned representations. How do central vision and temporal slowness, separately and jointly, affect the different facets of object semantics (basic category, fine-grained category, instance identity, and context of occurrence) when learning from human-like visual experience? And do the specific patterns of human eye movements matter for such learning?

taches.questions:
3D object annotation, which provides semantic labels and descriptions for 3D data, is crucial in computer vision and underpins applications such as autonomous driving, robotics, and augmented reality. Unlike 2D annotation, 3D annotation faces unique difficulties: increased complexity of spatial relationships, occlusion, and viewpoint variations that undermine cross-view consistency. Existing methods primarily rely on a single large-scale model, which struggles with complex objects and scenes: a single model must handle viewpoint differences, geometric complexity, and semantic consistency simultaneously. When objects are partially occluded or visible only from certain angles, existing methods often produce incomplete or inconsistent annotations. Approaches built on vision-language models frequently suffer from hallucinations and inconsistencies between descriptions, struggle to keep descriptions consistent across perspectives when using multi-view information, and often overlook the intrinsic geometric information of the object by relying solely on 2D images.

At its core, high-quality 3D annotation requires optimizing several competing objectives at once: accuracy, completeness, consistency, and efficiency. A single decision-making system often struggles to balance these goals, much like a solitary expert lacking proficiency across all domains. This raises a central question: how can an annotation system examine an object from several specialized perspectives, as a team of human experts would, covering geometric recognition, semantic understanding, and cross-view consistency? Answering it raises further difficulties. Decisions drawn from different sources of evidence must be reconciled under uncertainty and conflicting information, and fixed, predefined rules may not adapt to the diversity of object types and viewing conditions. It is also unclear how to define signals that reliably evaluate annotation quality without human labels, how to detect descriptions that are not grounded in the object's actual geometry, and how to achieve all of this at a cost and throughput compatible with annotating very large 3D asset collections.

taches.questions:
Biological sequences, including DNA, RNA and proteins, encode the fundamental information of life. Modeling these sequences requires capturing not only local motifs but also global bidirectional dependencies, as distant tokens and elements often interact in ways that critically determine biological function. For example, amino acid residues may form structural or functional interactions across long sequence distances from both directions, and motifs in DNA/RNA frequently depend on upstream and downstream context. Methods limited to unidirectional modeling therefore struggle to capture the biological reality in which sequence meaning arises from bidirectional contextual information.

Autoregressive (AR) models have become a dominant paradigm in biological sequence generation because of their capacity for tractable, stable sequential modeling. However, their inherent unidirectionality imposes a fundamental constraint, limiting their ability to capture the global sequence semantics that are often crucial for interpreting biological sequences, and left-to-right generation can suffer from error propagation. Non-autoregressive (NAR) Transformers, in contrast, employ holistic bidirectional self-attention and can learn potent bidirectional representations that may better reflect the underlying biology. Despite these representational advantages, NAR models introduce practical and theoretical challenges: managing variable sequence lengths often requires auxiliary length predictors that are prone to errors, and NAR-specific objectives (such as connectionist temporal classification losses) create complex optimization landscapes that can lead to training instability and reduced scalability compared with AR models. These difficulties have so far hindered the full realization of bidirectional processing in biological sequence modeling.

The field thus faces a dichotomy between the generative stability and precision of AR models and the rich contextual understanding of NAR models. The open question is whether, and how, an autoregressive generator can be given access to global, bidirectional context about the sequence it is producing, so that it keeps the stability of sequential decoding while gaining the holistic awareness of bidirectional models, without inheriting the weaknesses of NAR generation.

De novo peptide sequencing from tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) data is a demanding and consequential instance of this problem. Here the goal is to infer an amino acid sequence directly from an observed spectrum, described by its list of peaks (mass-to-charge ratios and intensities), the precursor mass and the precursor charge. Peptide sequencing is pivotal in proteomics, with impact ranging from fundamental biology to drug development. Traditional database search methods falter with novel sequences, as in de novo antibody characterization, neoantigen discovery and metaproteomics, which makes inferring sequences directly from spectra indispensable. Deep learning has largely superseded early de novo methods, and Transformer models now define the state of the art: autoregressive systems have mostly pursued architectural refinements within the AR paradigm, while more recent non-autoregressive systems have been explored chiefly for speed, but face challenges with sequence length prediction and complex optimization. How to combine the strengths of both paradigms for accurate, robust biological sequence generation remains an open problem.

taches.questions:
Vision-language models (VLMs) capable of jointly processing visual and textual data have shown strong reasoning abilities. In particular, given an input sequence of multiple images collected across varying timepoints, temporal VLMs can characterize visual changes over time, a capability known as temporal understanding. For example, temporal VLMs can recognize human actions given a sequence of video frames and characterize disease progression given longitudinal medical images.

Models designed to perform temporal understanding tasks often demonstrate high overall performance; however, recent works have shown that such models may be affected by static feature biases, a phenomenon where models use static patterns (e.g. the image background or a particular object in the scene) as shortcuts when making predictions, rather than analyzing the dynamic visual changes occurring across the image sequence. As an illustrative example, consider videos from an activity recognition dataset with the class label "climbing tree", which depict people climbing up or down trees. A temporal VLM that relies on static feature biases may base predictions for this class solely on the presence of trees and foliage, rather than on the true motion patterns associated with a person climbing a tree. At inference time, the performance of such a model will depend heavily on whether the static feature is present; consequently, it is likely to make systematic prediction errors when classifying videos from other classes (e.g. "swinging on something") in which trees are prominently visible. Prior work has also observed that using just a single frame as input can yield high performance on multi-image temporal understanding tasks, and a range of approaches have been proposed for reducing model reliance on static feature biases during training, predominantly for background biases in video-based activity recognition, through novel optimization procedures or data augmentation strategies. These approaches focus on mitigation during training rather than on discovering which biases a given pretrained model has actually learned.

Identifying learned static feature biases that contribute to systematic prediction errors is critical prior to real-world model deployment, particularly in safety-critical settings such as healthcare, where models that process medical images across multiple timepoints are increasingly used. Traditional approaches for detecting such failure modes, which typically combine manual analysis with pixel-wise interpretability algorithms (e.g. GradCAM), require extensive human effort and are time-consuming to apply at scale, particularly as the length of the input sequence increases. This suggests the need for automated approaches; however, automatically identifying error-inducing static feature biases is challenging for two reasons. First, existing automated approaches for discovering systematic errors (such as Domino, George and Distilling Failures) are designed for non-temporal (e.g. single-image) settings. These approaches typically analyze model predictions on a labeled validation dataset and surface coherent groups of misclassified samples, treating each input sample as a single entity; in the temporal setting, collapsing an entire multi-image sequence into a single entity may provide inadequate granularity, especially because image-level static features are typically not annotated in temporal datasets and may be visible in only a subset of the images in a sequence. Second, quantitatively evaluating automated approaches in the temporal setting is complicated by the fact that the ground-truth static feature biases of pretrained models are typically unknown, so it is difficult to ascertain whether the biases extracted by an automated method are indeed accurate.

The problem is therefore the following. Given a trained temporal VLM and a labeled validation dataset associated with a downstream temporal classification task, how can one automatically discover static features that (i) are error-inducing, meaning that their presence within a sequence contributes to prediction errors on the task, and (ii) reflect a learned model bias, meaning that the model relies on them when making predictions, even when such features are unannotated and appear in only part of a sequence? How can the accuracy of the discovered biases be assessed rigorously and quantitatively, given that the true biases of trained models are generally unknown? And can knowledge of such biases help developers understand and address the resulting failure modes before deployment?

taches.questions:
Sampling molecular configurations from the Boltzmann distribution p(x) ∝ exp(-E(x)), where E(x) is the potential energy of a configuration x, is a foundational and long-standing challenge in statistical physics. The ability to generate samples according to this distribution is the foundation for determining many other observables, such as free energies and heat capacities, which govern real-world behaviour. Efficient Boltzmann sampling is therefore essential for progress in a large range of areas, from characterizing the function of biomolecules, to accelerating drug design, and discovering novel materials.

The difficulty of this task arises from the structure of the energy for molecules of interest. The energy landscape is high-dimensional and non-smooth with many local energy minima. These rugged energies severely challenge classical simulation-based methods such as Molecular Dynamics and Markov chain Monte Carlo, which easily become trapped in local minima and require a computationally inaccessible number of steps to mix between modes. These samplers generate many correlated samples, creating large inefficiencies, whereas an ideal sampler would generate i.i.d. samples from the target distribution.

Boltzmann Generators address this inefficiency by amortizing the cost: a generative model is trained, typically on a small and possibly biased dataset, to sample from a proposal p_theta(x) close to p(x), and its samples are then corrected to p(x) using self-normalized importance sampling. This correction requires efficient access to p_theta(x) and E(x) for every sample drawn, but in return guarantees statistical consistency of the corrected samples and allows inference-time scaling, since Monte Carlo estimates of observables converge to the correct values as the number of samples grows.

The main design choice in Boltzmann Generators is which type of generator to use. Modern Boltzmann Generators primarily use continuous normalizing flows, trained with flow matching, because of their expressive power, ease of training and flexibility of parameterization. However, while the likelihood of a continuous normalizing flow is accessible in principle, approximating it with sufficient accuracy is extremely costly, for two reasons: approximate trace estimators are not sufficiently accurate, so full Jacobian computations are needed at each step along the flow; and many integration steps are needed to control discretization error. Likelihood evaluation thus requires thousands of function evaluations per sample, which severely limits adoption and has confined existing continuous-flow Boltzmann Generators for molecules to small equivariant architectures of at most a few million parameters. Discrete normalizing flows, by contrast, offer fast one-step sampling with exact likelihoods, but they are slow and unstable to train with maximum likelihood and are constrained to inherently invertible architectures, which limits their expressivity and scalability.

Recently, there have been significant advances in few-step generation with flow models, such as consistency models and flow map models that learn an average velocity between a current and a target time. These models are powerful few-step generators with flexible architectures and efficient simulation-free training. However, they do not natively admit efficient estimators of the likelihood: the learned map is invertible at the optimum of its training objective, but there is no guarantee that it is invertible before that objective is perfectly minimized, which makes the standard change-of-variables formula inapplicable. They are therefore unsuitable, as they stand, for the high-precision demands of importance sampling and scientific applications such as Boltzmann generation.

This raises the central question: how can one design a generative model that combines the training efficiency and architectural freedom of simulation-free flow models with the fast sampling and likelihood evaluation of discrete-time invertible models, so that it generates samples in a few steps while providing likelihoods that are both cheap to compute and accurate enough for importance sampling? Answering it would make Boltzmann Generators far more practical.

taches.questions:
Machine learning and statistical learning rely on data, but data are always finite and, in some application areas, rather limited. This inevitably creates uncertainty in estimation, representation and prediction, which needs to be quantified. Approaches to uncertainty quantification can be coarsely divided into frequentist and Bayesian frameworks. The frequentist framework treats the data as random and the parameters as fixed but unknown; uncertainty arises from the randomness of the data, and the reliance on the distribution of an estimator yields desirable long-run guarantees, such as coverage of the true parameters and valid predictive coverage. The Bayesian framework treats the parameters as random and the data as fixed: a prior distribution expressing the modeler's beliefs is updated by conditioning on the data, and the resulting posterior, read as updated beliefs, is conventionally interpreted as uncertainty quantification. In short, frequentist statistics has valid behavioral properties, while Bayesian statistics has valid belief updating.

Because it does not depend on theoretical populations and offers easily interpreted, belief-based uncertainty, Bayesian statistics has become especially appealing in machine and deep learning, and efficient algorithms for sampling from posterior distributions have been developed. Yet, in the over-parametrized setting of most modern applications, it is unclear how priors should be chosen and, more importantly, how a posterior over an over-parametrized parameter space should be interpreted. Prior work has already questioned Bayesian neural networks on predictive grounds, showing that predictive performance improves when the evidence is overcounted, which violates the information-processing optimality of Bayesian updating; this can be justified by the safe Bayesian paradigm when the model class is misspecified.

The usual reassurance that Bayesian and frequentist inference agree comes from the Bernstein-von Mises theorem: for finite-dimensional parameter spaces, the posterior asymptotically becomes a Gaussian centered at the maximum likelihood estimate, the data dominate the prior, and credible intervals acquire valid frequentist coverage. In modern machine learning, however, the size of the dataset is at best of the same order as the number of parameters and often much smaller, which makes this result of limited relevance, if not void. The prior therefore strongly shapes the posterior, while there is no clear guidance on how to choose it; moreover, the goal is usually optimal prediction rather than modeling a true data-generating process, which may not even exist. Frequentist approaches face their own difficulties: the estimators of modern models are hard to analyze even asymptotically and harder still with finite data, bootstrapping is often inadequate because of long training procedures and small datasets, and frequentist guarantees typically assume a correctly specified model class. Recent work has also shown that Bayesian updating can be written as an optimization over probability measures, minimizing an expected loss plus a divergence to the prior, with the Bayes rule as the solution for the negative log-likelihood loss and the Kullback-Leibler divergence.

This raises several questions. Does a Bayesian posterior, or the predictive distribution derived from it, deliver uncertainty statements that are valid in a frequentist, long-run sense, particularly when data are scarce relative to the number of parameters, the prior is influential, or the model is misspecified? If not, what do such posteriors actually represent? How could the quality of a prior be judged by an external criterion rather than by the modeler's beliefs? And can predictive intervals derived from a Bayesian posterior be made to achieve valid frequentist coverage without requiring a correctly specified model?

taches.questions:
Key moments of a video can occur at any time, exemplified by soccer, where game-deciding moments typically span seconds of a 90-minute game. Within those moments, split-second actions define the outcome: an assist, a missed tackle, the movement of the keeper. Multimodal large language models have achieved substantial progress in vision-language perception and reasoning, but still cannot match the human ability to extract and reason about salient moments in videos. While humans naturally sample color visuals at around 60 Hz across large contexts, existing vision-language models often sample a single frame per second, so they often miss key transition frames and struggle to maintain coherence across long time scales. Intuitively, increasing the context for these models by sampling more frames improves accuracy, particularly for long videos and complex reasoning tasks. However, this pays for improvement with additional tokens, increasing computational complexity and pushing against the fundamental limits of model context.

To address these challenges, many approaches adopt token compression to reduce redundancy and increase informative context. However, when applied to complex reasoning tasks, compression-based models perform worse than full-token methods, and compression strategies often limit generalization through reduced perception and reasoning capacity; such compression can cause irreversible information loss on complex tasks without removing the computational and latency bottlenecks of the language model. Sparse attention mechanisms offer a different trade-off: they preserve tokens but focus the model's capacity on the relevant dependencies between tokens. Numerous sparse attention methods have been employed in large language models, but most are optimized for text or short multimodal contexts and are inadequate for the ultra-long, highly redundant spatio-temporal structure of video; training-free variants are rarely hardware-aligned and do not improve training efficiency.

This raises several open questions. Can video-language models be made to scale to much longer vision contexts at a small fraction of the cost of dense attention, without sacrificing long-video understanding, fine-grained temporal reasoning, or spatial fidelity? Under a fixed token or attention budget, how should capacity be allocated between temporal density and per-frame spatial resolution, and between global and local attention? Does a model trained at one context length extrapolate beyond it? And how does sparsifying attention interact with known pathologies of decoder-only transformers, such as attention sinks, where a disproportionate amount of attention mass is absorbed by a few tokens as a byproduct of softmax normalization: do sparsity patterns amplify or mitigate such sinks?

taches.questions:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have recently emerged as a promising alternative to dense large language models (LLMs), replacing dense feed-forward layers with sparsely activated experts and dynamic routing. This design allows MoE models to match or surpass the performance of dense LLMs while activating only a fraction of parameters during inference, making them particularly attractive for large-scale, concurrent deployment. However, while sparse activation reduces computational cost, it exacerbates memory requirements. For example, DeepSeek-V3 activates only 37B parameters per inference, yet all 671B parameters must still be stored in GPU memory, resulting in prohibitively high deployment costs. MoE layers typically account for over 97% of total model parameters and represent the dominant storage bottleneck. Compressing MoE layers is therefore critical to overcoming inference inefficiency and making deployment feasible on resource-constrained devices.

Model pruning has been widely explored as a compression strategy to reduce storage and improve efficiency. Yet a fundamental trade-off persists: fine-grained pruning typically preserves accuracy but yields limited speedups on hardware, whereas coarse-grained pruning directly enables acceleration but often incurs obvious accuracy loss. Within MoE models, unstructured parameter sparsification faces similar limitations, as hardware inefficiencies constrain its practical benefits.

Consequently, recent research has shifted toward expert-level pruning, which offers more direct gains in both acceleration and memory reduction. Existing expert-level approaches can be broadly divided into expert dropping and expert merging. Expert dropping methods completely remove experts deemed unimportant, but relying solely on a calibration set to discard entire experts risks losing valuable complementary expertise, often leading to notable performance degradation and to overfitting to the calibration data. Expert merging methods instead aim to consolidate functionally similar experts to better preserve overall model capacity; however, their clustering-based similarity measures are unstable, limited similarity between experts makes them prone to parameter conflicts, and naive merging strategies (e.g., averaging or frequency-based weighting) often introduce destructive conflicts, resulting in suboptimal outcomes. Decomposition-based approaches represent individual experts as a mixture of shared and specialized components (for instance through weighted combinations, low-rank residuals or SVD-based shared subspaces); while this helps preserve model capacity, it requires computationally expensive decomposition and merging operations, some methods require additional fine-tuning for recovery, and a non-negligible accuracy loss remains.

This leaves an open problem. Is there a pruning unit inside MoE layers that is more flexible and finer-grained than an entire expert, so that pruning can better preserve accuracy, yet structured enough to deliver real reductions in memory and computation on standard hardware? And for such units, how can one quantify the importance of each unit to the model's overall performance in a principled way, without retraining, and at a cost that remains affordable for MoE models with tens of billions of parameters? Principled saliency criteria such as the classical Optimal Brain Surgeon framework approximate the effect of removing weights via a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss, identifying parameters with minimal contribution, but estimating the Hessian is computationally prohibitive for modern deep architectures. Even the layer-wise Hessian estimation that has become widely adopted for pruning large models would, at the level of a single expert, require space complexity of $\mathcal{O}\left((3d_{\text{model}} \cdot d_{\text{inter}})^2 \right)$, where $d_{\text{model}}$ is the hidden size of the model and $d_{\text{inter}}$ the intermediate dimension of an expert, which is still unacceptable. The challenge is thus to obtain an accurate, loss-aware importance measure for sub-expert pruning units whose computation and storage remain tractable.

taches.questions:
Multi-View Stereo (MVS) aims to reconstruct dense 3D geometry of objects or scenes from calibrated multi-view images, and is widely used in fields such as autonomous driving. It estimates the depth of each pixel of a reference image by identifying correspondences across source views that satisfy multi-view geometric consistency, which makes the task highly dependent on the quality of feature matching: more robust feature representations lead to more reliable matching.

Traditional MVS methods rely on handcrafted features, which tend to perform poorly in regions with repetitive patterns, weak textures and reflections. Learning-based MVS methods have made significant strides by leveraging the representational power of deep neural networks, and coarse-to-fine methods built on feature pyramid networks have become the dominant paradigm. Early learning-based methods use convolutional neural networks and their variants for feature extraction, but their limited receptive fields restrict them to local features. More recently, Transformers have been introduced to model long-range dependencies, enabling global feature learning both within and across views and improving the robustness of matching in challenging regions.

Despite this progress, Transformer-based MVS methods suffer from quadratic computational complexity. Existing mitigations include linear attention, attention restricted to epipolar-aligned windows, and vanilla attention restricted to epipolar line pairs, typically applied only at the lowest-resolution stage. These approaches still require multiple alternating rounds of self-attention and cross-attention across reference and source features, which incurs substantial overhead; other methods enhance features with parameter-heavy pretrained vision Transformers. Striking a good balance between reconstruction quality and efficiency (memory, runtime and parameter count) therefore remains a major challenge, especially for high-resolution images and many input views. Moreover, MVS is inherently a one-to-many matching problem, in which a single reference view must be related to several source views, so global feature aggregation must capture both intra-view and inter-view dependencies.

The central question is: how can an MVS network aggregate global, long-range intra- and inter-view feature dependencies across multiple views so as to sustain high reconstruction accuracy and completeness, and generalize to unseen real-world scenes, while minimizing computational cost?

taches.questions:
Large language models have achieved unprecedented performance, fueled by web-scale text resources, substantial computational power, and billions of parameters. In the multimodal domain, large multimodal models and visual generative models have also demonstrated exceptional capabilities in tasks such as general-purpose visual question answering and text-to-image/video generation. Given their success, unified multimodal models have been investigated to unify multimodal understanding and generation within a single model or system, seeking to cultivate both abilities simultaneously through pre-training, fine-tuning, or connecting tailored models.

Existing unified models can be characterized along two perspectives. First, regarding visual representations, some works (e.g., Chameleon, Transfusion, Show-o) use a single unified representation for both understanding and generation, while others use decoupled representations, typically a CLIP-style encoder for understanding and a variational autoencoder for generation. Second, regarding the type of unification, one family natively applies multimodal understanding and generation objectives within a single model (native unified multimodal models), while another assembles off-the-shelf specialized multimodal models and visual generators by tuning adapters or learnable tokens. These principles are combined with autoregressive modeling, diffusion modeling, or both. Related evidence from multimodal understanding suggests that encoder-free models that align raw visual features directly in the language model embedding space often fall behind models that use image-text-aligned visual features.

Two open problems motivate this work. First, existing unified models primarily focus on text and images; it remains unclear how to design a native unified model whose visual representation scales across both image and video modalities while serving both understanding and generation. This is challenging because multimodal understanding and generation differ in their feature dependencies: understanding benefits from rich, high-level semantic information, whereas generation requires low-level features that preserve intrinsic structure and fine details, and for videos these must also be handled consistently over time.

Second, existing unified models are typically trained from language models, large multimodal models, or from scratch, aiming to cultivate visual generative capabilities while preserving language modeling proficiency. This often relies on web-scale, high-quality text corpora, which are prohibitively expensive to collect; without such resources, language knowledge and modeling performance can degrade. How can visual generation ability be added to a pre-trained language model that lacks it, while retaining its language knowledge and without requiring a massive text corpus? And how can such a training procedure be made efficient enough to scale to larger language models?

taches.questions:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a powerful paradigm for learning on structured data, yet their expressive power is fundamentally limited by the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) hierarchy. In particular, message-passing GNNs struggle to capture higher-order topological signals (for example, the presence, interaction, and disappearance of cycles) that often drive downstream performance in molecular learning, physical systems, and network science. Persistent Homology (PH) from Topological Data Analysis offers a way to extract such signals by tracking the life of topological features along a filtration. Accordingly, PH-based descriptors are increasingly used to augment GNNs and higher-order neural architectures, and to boost their expressivity.

However, many PH pipelines in graph learning rely on inclusion-based filtrations ("forward persistence"), which traverse an increasing sequence of subgraphs. This one-sided view can leave information on the table. In a forward pass on a graph, a cycle that is born can never die, while new connected components can keep appearing as vertices arrive. This is also undesirable from the perspective of metrizability: the bottleneck distance between the persistence diagrams of two different graphs can be infinite, because the two graphs may have different numbers of permanent, never-dying features. Workarounds such as forcing all permanent features to die at an arbitrary finite time after the filtration ends are sensitive to that arbitrary choice, since many features may then die around the same artificial time. Within the PH literature, extended persistence, which considers both a forward and a reverse pass over the input data, is one known way to resolve the metrizability problem, and it has been used in GNNs; other constructions such as zigzag filtrations also combine different filtration directions.

This raises several open questions. Which principled topological operations, beyond inclusions, can assign finite lifetimes to features that would otherwise persist forever, and how do the resulting descriptors compare in expressive power with forward persistence and with extended persistence? Must the order in which pieces of a graph enter the process follow a single fixed filtration, or can more flexible schedules extract more information? Can such descriptors retain stability guarantees with respect to perturbations of the input filtrations, and yield well-defined distances between diagrams of different graphs? Can they be computed efficiently, made learnable end-to-end inside differentiable GNN pipelines, and generalized beyond graphs to the simplicial and cellular complexes used by higher-order topological networks? Finally, can they help with the difficulty PH-based methods face in scaling to large inputs?

taches.questions:
Solving partial differential equations (PDEs) is a cornerstone of modeling and simulating complex phenomena in science and engineering. In computational fluid dynamics, PDEs are the primary framework for describing fluid behavior, relating variables such as velocity and pressure to the system's evolution over time. Traditional numerical methods, including finite difference, finite volume and finite element methods, provide high-fidelity results but often require significant computational resources, a cost that becomes prohibitive when simulations must be repeated across wide parameter variations or for real-time applications. Machine and deep learning approaches have emerged as promising alternatives. Discrete data-driven methods represent PDE solutions directly with neural networks tailored to specific equations and discretizations, using convolutional, residual and graph architectures to encode spatial information and evolve solutions over time, while physics-informed frameworks (PINNs and their variants) enable unsupervised and semi-supervised recovery of single-instance solutions. These neural solvers, however, handle discretization poorly and depend on the system configuration. Continuous frameworks such as neural operators and DeepONet instead learn mappings between function spaces; the Fourier Neural Operator uses the fast Fourier transform to achieve discretization invariance, and extensions have adapted neural operators to complex geometries or to parametric and physics-informed settings, yet they still face limited generalization.

Attention has therefore shifted toward Scientific Foundation Models: data-driven models trained on a broad distribution of physical systems, meant to generalize across scientific problems and conditions without retraining from scratch, and to serve as reusable bases that remove the need for a dedicated solver for each PDE type. Two paradigms dominate. One conditions solution prediction on the symbolic form of the governing PDE, treating mathematical expressions as structured sequences analogous to text and encoding them jointly with numerical solution data (for example PROSE, fine-tuned large language models, or Unified Pretrained Solvers). The other relies solely on simulation data and learns to predict future states from past observations, through in-context learning (VICON), block-causal or multiscale operator transformers (BCAT, Poseidon), pretraining across multiple PDE systems (MPP), or large-scale autoregressive modeling inspired by video transformers (PhysiX).

Despite their promise, these models face notable challenges. Pretraining on massive, heterogeneous physics datasets requires large volumes of expensive simulation data and substantial computational resources, and the resulting models typically rely on opaque latent representations that offer little physical interpretability and make it unclear how knowledge about one physical system can be reused for another. The difficulty is sharpest for multi-dimensional, strongly coupled systems such as the two-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, where the velocity evolves under nonlinear convection and viscous diffusion while the pressure enforces a global divergence-free constraint; numerical solvers handle this pressure-velocity coupling through costly iterative procedures.

This raises several questions. Can a learned surrogate for PDEs reuse previously acquired physical knowledge when adapting to new, coupled systems, instead of relearning everything within a single monolithic model? How can such a surrogate respect the constraints of the governing equations, including incompressibility, rather than only fitting data? And can it do so with limited data and parameters, remain stable over long autoregressive rollouts where errors accumulate, offer physical interpretability, and run substantially faster than traditional numerical solvers?

taches.questions:
Reconstructing high-fidelity 3D human representations and understanding human body and clothing attributes are a fundamental challenge in 3D vision. Doing both together could unlock many practical downstream applications, such as semantic-guided 3D reasoning, context-aware human behavior analysis, and interactive semantic editing, and would further facilitate immersive augmented and virtual reality, character stylization, and cinematic production.

Neural Radiance Fields have enabled high-quality synthesis of novel views of humans, but implicit representations are typically computationally intensive because they rely on dense point querying in 3D space. 3D Gaussian Splatting provides real-time rendering of explicit human models, yet existing human Gaussian methods rely on dense multi-view images or monocular video together with time-consuming per-subject optimization, which limits their stability and feasibility in downstream applications. Large reconstruction models trained on large-scale 3D object datasets can directly regress 3D representations in a feed-forward manner, but on humans they tend to fail to produce faithful and consistent novel views, largely because 3D human data is scarce and because their designs lack human prior knowledge as an inductive bias. Generalizable human-specific reconstruction methods have enabled robust synthesis under sparse-view settings, but they address appearance only.

Meanwhile, semantic understanding of humans in 3D, such as body-part segmentation, is hindered by the lack of large, well-labeled 3D human datasets. Powerful 2D human-centric foundation models segment human parts well in images, but they lack 3D constraints and cannot by themselves deliver coherent segmentation across viewpoints. Work on scenes has embedded semantics into radiance fields and Gaussian feature fields, and has lifted 2D features to 3D, but the human-specific domain remains largely unexplored. An obvious workaround is to first reconstruct a 3D human and then apply a 2D human segmentation model to rendered views; such two-stage pipelines involve long processing times and substantial engineering effort, and per-view 2D operations do not guarantee 3D consistency across viewpoints, raising problems of inconsistency, computational cost and scalability.

This raises the central question: can a single model, given only one image of a person, produce in a single feed-forward pass a 3D human representation that supports both photorealistic novel-view rendering and 3D-consistent human-part segmentation? Answering it requires overcoming the scarcity of labeled 3D human part data, injecting appropriate human-specific inductive biases, and determining whether appearance reconstruction and semantic segmentation can reinforce rather than compete with each other when learned jointly, all while remaining fast enough for interactive use.

taches.questions:
Visual foundation models (VFMs) trained with self-supervised learning on large image datasets have become a powerful tool for a wide range of computer vision tasks. Techniques such as contrastive learning and self-distillation (e.g., DINO and DINOv2) allow these models to learn high-quality visual representations without manual labels. Despite their generality, performance can suffer when they are applied to specialized domains whose characteristics differ from the pre-training data, especially under distribution shift and label scarcity. For this reason, after a VFM is pre-trained, fine-tuning is commonly employed before applying it to downstream tasks. Supervised fine-tuning has been the dominant approach, with impressive results across applications such as remote sensing, medical imaging and place recognition. These successes demonstrate the adaptability of pre-trained models, but also highlight their reliance on labeled data, which can be expensive or impractical to obtain in many real-world scenarios.

Significant challenges arise in scenarios where labeled data are unavailable for supervised fine-tuning. Despite its potential in cases where collecting annotations is costly, time-consuming, or even infeasible, unsupervised fine-tuning of foundation models remains largely underexplored in vision. By contrast, the natural language processing community has long adopted unsupervised fine-tuning as a standard way to specialize large language models to new data distributions, typically via continued pretraining on unlabeled in-domain text. While this strategy has proven successful for generative language models, it has not proven effective for vision-centric encoder models, and its adaptation to visual data remains an open and challenging problem.

Prior work frames the gap. Many approaches for adapting vision foundation models, such as adapter modules or visual prompt tuning, rely on supervised learning and often involve complex adaptation pipelines. Continual self-supervised pretraining has been used to build new domain-specific foundation models (for instance for satellite imagery), but these models still rely on supervised fine-tuning to complete the adaptation. Domain adaptation methods based on self-supervision typically assume a labeled source domain and an unlabeled target domain, rather than adapting a pretrained model with unlabeled target data alone. Separately, videos provide rich supervisory signals through their spatio-temporal consistency, natural motion and realistic object transformations, and several works have investigated transferring knowledge from video to image representations; however, these often involve costly frame selection pipelines, hybrid loss formulations, substantial architectural modifications and training instability, mostly target pixel-level tasks, and show limited improvements for frame-level classification. Finally, continuing self-supervised training from a pretrained foundation model is delicate in itself: shifts in the data distribution can destabilize training and degrade the pretrained representations, so that the model quickly forgets its pretrained knowledge and reaches a degraded state.

A few natural questions therefore arise. How can a pre-trained vision foundation model be adapted to a specific context or domain without any supervision? What forms of unlabeled visual data are best suited for adapting vision foundation models to new data distributions? And what type of learning technique can effectively adapt pre-trained visual representations under these constraints, improving downstream performance in the target domain without disrupting the knowledge encoded during pretraining?
