taches.questions:
We consider the task of learning to generate samples X in R^N from an unnormalized target distribution pi_0(X) = exp(-E(X))/Z, where the energy function E can be evaluated but the partition function Z is unknown and computationally intractable, and where no samples from the target are available. Sampling problems of this kind are fundamental challenges in computational physics and chemistry and in Bayesian inference. Recent approaches train probability distributions parameterized by neural networks to approximate such targets: early deep-learning methods used exact-likelihood models such as normalizing flows and autoregressive models, while more recent work has turned to approximate-likelihood models such as diffusion models, in both continuous and discrete domains. In the continuous domain, the first diffusion samplers learned to reverse fixed forward processes given by variance-preserving or variance-exploding stochastic differential equations (SDEs). More recently, diffusion bridge samplers, in which the forward process is learnable as well, have established a new state of the art.

Such samplers are typically trained by minimizing a divergence between the joint distributions of the diffusion paths under the forward and reverse processes. This choice is motivated by the data processing inequality: for f-divergences, the divergence between the intractable marginal distributions is upper bounded by the divergence between the tractable path distributions, so that reducing the latter tightens a bound on the former, much like maximizing an evidence lower bound in latent variable models. In practice, two losses dominate: (i) the reverse Kullback-Leibler (rKL) divergence with gradients computed via the reparameterization trick, and (ii) the Log Variance (LV) loss, which does not require backpropagation through an expectation and is known as the trajectory balance loss in the GFlowNet literature. Both come with significant practical difficulties. The reparameterized rKL loss is susceptible to vanishing and exploding gradients when many diffusion steps are used, and it has been empirically reported to underperform the LV loss, an observation commonly attributed to the mode-seeking behaviour of the reverse KL divergence. Conversely, diffusion bridge samplers trained with the LV loss are prone to training instabilities and need extensive hyperparameter tuning; earlier work even reported poor performance and numerical instabilities when the LV loss was applied to diffusion bridges. Moreover, the LV loss is not an f-divergence, so it is unclear whether it inherits the conceptual footing that the data processing inequality provides for divergence-based losses. For samplers whose forward process is fixed, the on-policy LV loss is known to be closely related to the reverse KL objective, but whether such relations persist when forward-process parameters, parameters shared between the two processes, or the diffusion coefficients themselves are learned has not been examined. The choice of diffusion coefficients is itself delicate: they control how much stochasticity is injected and thus govern a trade-off between exploring multimodal targets and sampling precisely, and the appropriate noise level may differ across problems and even across dimensions of one problem.

This raises the following questions. Is the LV loss a well-founded and reliable objective for training diffusion bridge samplers, in particular when forward-process parameters or diffusion coefficients are learned? Is there a training objective and gradient estimator for diffusion bridges that keeps the theoretical justification of divergence-based losses while avoiding both the gradient pathologies of the reparameterization trick and the instability and hyperparameter sensitivity of the LV loss? And can diffusion coefficients be learned jointly with the drifts to improve sampling quality without destabilizing training?

taches.questions:
Language models have evolved from static knowledge bases into agents capable of complex reasoning and problem-solving, a shift driven largely by post-training and test-time scaling methods. While test-time scaling is training-free, post-training generally yields higher performance gains at a lower inference budget, and the effectiveness and efficiency of post-training have become a primary focus of research. Of the two prominent post-training paradigms, supervised fine-tuning is computationally cheap but limited by the difficulty of curating high-quality, comprehensive datasets, whereas reinforcement learning, which optimizes the model against a reward signal from human preferences or from external verification (reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, RLVR), can explore a broader action space and achieves superior performance on complex, open-ended tasks. RLVR in particular has become popular because it relies little on human input.

This performance comes at a significant computational cost. Proximal Policy Optimization requires training a separate value model, which is prohibitively memory-intensive in resource-constrained settings. Critic-free, group-based methods such as GRPO, Dr. GRPO and RLOO avoid the value model by estimating the advantage relative to a group of rollouts sampled for the same prompt, but they must generate many rollouts per training prompt; the group size typically has to be large (e.g., 16) for stable training, which exacerbates generation overhead and leads to a memory-bound system. Sampling efficiency has therefore become a key bottleneck. Moreover, these methods allocate the same fixed number of rollouts to every training prompt, implicitly treating all prompts as equally informative, which may waste the computational budget and slow training progress.

Prior work has attacked the performance-cost trade-off from several angles. Hybrid approaches combine or merge supervised fine-tuning and RL stages, smoothing or accelerating training, but they do not adapt to the model's evolving ability to solve the training problems. It has been observed that filtering out prompts on which the model's accuracy is close to 0 or 1 improves training, since such prompts produce rollout groups with zero reward variance and contribute no gradient signal; related methods filter rollouts with low absolute advantage or retain the highest-variance examples. Lacking an a priori measure of prompt informativeness, however, these methods must pre-sample a large batch of rollouts before each update, which can negate the efficiency gains. Other works estimate informativeness before sampling, for example by skipping prompts that were recently non-informative, by drawing a small trial batch to screen prompts, by predicting difficulty from past rewards or learned predictors, or by assigning larger budgets to difficult prompts or selecting prompts matched to the model's current competence. These are largely heuristic: there is still a lack of principled metrics that capture how much a prompt's rollouts actually help the policy update, and consequently a lack of an adaptive control mechanism for group-based policy optimization.

This raises several questions. Given a hard total rollout budget per training batch, how should rollouts be distributed among the prompts of the batch, rather than uniformly, to make the policy update as useful as possible? What per-prompt quantity should such an allocation be based on? Because a prompt's informativeness cannot be observed before sampling and drifts as the model weights change after every update, how can it be estimated ahead of time for each prompt, cheaply and reliably? And how can the resulting allocation decision be computed quickly enough, respecting the total budget, that its overhead is negligible relative to rollout generation and policy updates?

taches.questions:
Recent advances in large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have transformed tasks at the intersection of vision and text. Building on their success with static images, attention has shifted to the more challenging domain of video understanding, which requires reasoning over complex temporal dynamics and visual narratives, and powerful foundation VLMs are now being adapted to tasks such as Video Question Answering (VideoQA).

A critical challenge in video understanding is the perception bottleneck. Long videos contain so many frames that processing the entire video is computationally infeasible and exceeds the limited context windows of VLMs. Foundation VLMs therefore resort to frame sampling, most commonly uniform sampling at a fixed interval. Although uniform sampling maximizes temporal coverage, its content-agnostic nature tends to select redundant frames while omitting crucial, query-relevant moments.

A prominent line of research addresses this through query-related frame selection. Many such approaches rely on lightweight multi-modal models like CLIP to compute a query-frame similarity that then guides a selection algorithm. However, complex queries, for instance asking what a video's creator introduced after a particular segment, require temporal reasoning and holistic semantic understanding. Lightweight models lack these capabilities and tend to treat the query as a bag of keywords: they may assign high similarity to frames that merely share the query's context or are visually similar to a keyword, while ranking lower the frame that actually contains the answer because it has a weaker surface-level association with the query's words. The resulting similarity scores fail to reflect true query-frame relevance, and the selection built on them fails.

By analogy with human perception, relying on a lightweight model resembles quickly glancing over a video, which may lack the attention needed for complex situations. Another family of methods instead employs VLMs as analyzers of each query-frame pair, which is closer to carefully examining every frame: an analysis VLM produces a relevance score using its strong comprehension of complex queries, and an answering VLM then answers from the selected frames. Such methods include training-free approaches that use proprietary models to generate captions or agents for reflective analysis, and training-based approaches that fine-tune a VLM to select frames or jointly train a localizer and an answerer. This deep analysis, however, comes at a staggering computational cost: an 8B-scale VLM can take more than a second to analyze a single frame, so methods that analyze an initial set of 128 frames in a single pass incur a cost on the order of minutes per query. While VLM-based analysis is highly effective, its cost renders it impractical for many real-world applications.

Current frame selection methods thus face a critical trade-off between the poor relevance estimates of lightweight similarity models on complex queries and the prohibitive cost of exhaustive VLM-based analysis. The open problem is how to select, for a given video and query, a concise yet comprehensive set of frames that captures the query-relevant moments, including those that a lightweight similarity model would miss, while keeping the amount of expensive VLM computation small, so that the selected frames measurably improve the question-answering accuracy of off-the-shelf VLMs.

taches.questions:
Representation learning lies at the heart of modern machine learning. The successes of large-scale unsupervised pre-training have shown that rich representations can enable both efficient adaptation and strong generalization across tasks. An important class of reinforcement learning problems where representations matter is goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, whose objective is to train a multi-task policy capable of reaching any target state from any starting state in minimal time. Many real-world tasks, including navigation, object manipulation, and even games, naturally fit into this goal-reaching framework, and in the offline setting such policies must be learned purely from a fixed, reward-free dataset of trajectories, without any interaction with the environment.

An important open question in goal-conditioned reinforcement learning is how to represent goals. Many works simply use the original state observations provided by the environment to represent goal states, but these observations are not necessarily best structured to describe goals (that is, tasks), and they often contain superfluous information, such as uncontrollable noise or background variation that does not affect goal reaching. A good, well-designed goal representation, by contrast, could accelerate policy learning during training by providing structured information about the goal, improve goal-reaching performance at test time, and potentially enable robust generalization to unseen or out-of-distribution goals.

What constitutes an ideal goal representation? Two desiderata are natural. First, the representation must capture enough information about the goal to represent an optimal goal-conditioned policy (sufficiency). Second, it must be able to discard information that is irrelevant to goal reaching, such as exogenous noise in the observations (noise invariance). In other words, an ideal goal representation would retain only a necessary and sufficient amount of information for optimal goal reaching, letting the agent focus on the controllable part of the state.

Prior work on representation learning for reinforcement learning has proposed many techniques, such as bisimulation, contrastive and self-predictive objectives, and successor representations or features (which are defined with respect to a fixed policy rather than optimal behavior). Within goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, previous methods learn temporal-distance embeddings with metric parameterizations, information-bottleneck goal encoders, behavioral temporal contrastive representations, or temporal self-predictive representations, and often use these embeddings for skill learning, state representations, reward shaping, or planning rather than specifically as goal representations. It remains unclear which notion of goal representation provably satisfies both sufficiency and noise invariance, and how it could be learned in practice from offline data with continuous, high-dimensional observations, in a form that can be combined with any existing offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning algorithm.

taches.questions:
Tables are a fundamental medium for storing and communicating information across domains such as finance, scientific communication, biomedical records, and the web. Unlocking the knowledge contained in these tables has motivated extensive research on Table Question Answering (Table QA), where models answer natural language queries grounded in tabular data. In practice, tables appear both in structured formats, with rigid schemas that support executable SQL queries, and in semi-structured formats, where columns are irregular, may be merged or repurposed, and cells contain free text, lists or other long-form content. Structured tables enable precision and symbolic reasoning, while semi-structured tables offer robustness to noise and incomplete metadata. Since both formats coexist in real-world settings, understanding their impact on Table QA methods is crucial.

Despite substantial progress, a key question remains unanswered: how do different modeling paradigms handle variation in table representation? Existing benchmarks focus on query domain or complexity, but fix the table format itself. As a result, models are optimized for a single representation, leaving their robustness to representation shift unclear. Current approaches fall into three main families: NL2SQL methods, which translate questions into executable SQL; LLM-based methods, which reason directly over the table; and hybrid methods, which combine symbolic execution with neural reasoning. NL2SQL methods scale and reason precisely but are known to be brittle under noisy or irregular schemas. LLM-based methods can handle semi-structured inputs containing free text but struggle on complex queries and long tables. Hybrid methods aim to balance flexibility and precision. A central difficulty is that comparing behavior across formats is confounded: when structured and semi-structured benchmarks contain different information, differences in performance may simply reflect content mismatches rather than the effect of representation itself. No prior work has isolated the effect of semi-structured representations under the same information conditions, and most analytical studies evaluate a single family of methods in isolation.

Representation is also entangled with other factors that are known to affect performance. Large tables strain context windows, make relevant rows hard to locate, and expose the difficulty language models have with exact numerical comparisons across many values. Multi-table questions require aligning schemas and linking rows across tables, which is harder when explicit keys are absent. Queries range from simple lookups to multi-step reasoning involving aggregation, filtering, comparisons and arithmetic, and it remains unclear how methods scale from one to the other across representations. Finally, while curated databases maintain consistent schemas, real-world tables often have missing headers, inconsistent formatting and absent metadata, noise that can severely affect symbolic methods. Prior insights about table length, multi-table reasoning and query complexity remain fragmented across benchmarks, and their interaction with representation has not been systematically examined.

This raises several questions. How does performance vary across modeling paradigms when structured and semi-structured inputs carry identical content? How do methods scale from short to long tables? How do multi-table alignment and join operations affect performance? How does performance change from simple lookups to multi-step compositional queries? How robust are methods under noisy or incomplete schemas? Without a controlled evaluation of representation effects, practitioners lack guidance on method selection, and researchers risk overfitting to narrow benchmark conditions.

taches.questions:
There are many ways to segment a biomedical image. Depending on their goals, clinicians or biomedical researchers employ a specific segmentation protocol, which defines the regions of interest to be segmented. A brain MRI, for instance, could be segmented into major anatomical classes, granular anatomical regions, diffuse tissue types, vascular territories or other systemic structures such as vessels or nerves, pathologies, or functional areas.

Existing learning-based biomedical image segmentation tools all require the protocol to be specified. Fully automated models are trained on image-segmentation pairs, which implicitly fix a single protocol: the one they were trained on. In-context or few-shot models also use image-segmentation pairs, but take them as input to specify the desired protocol for a target image. Interactive models rely on user clicks, boxes, scribbles or text to indicate the desired regions. In every case the protocol is specified by the user, interactively or by example, which is a substantial burden on biomedical researchers who commonly need to segment a new collection of images, often with a new protocol, and for whom annotating enough examples or prompting every image is labor-intensive. New protocols are frequently introduced, and researchers studying how anatomy relates to outcomes or predictors may want to explore candidate regions that have never been segmented before.

Some universal models can automatically partition an image from a new biomedical domain into multiple labels without prompting. However, such partitions are produced image by image: the same label index can have different meanings in different images, and when the same structure is segmented in two images it usually receives different label indices. Establishing correspondence after the fact is non-trivial, because different images may be partitioned on entirely different bases. Yet consistency is critical whenever the same set of structures must be analyzed across many subjects, as in population and longitudinal studies. Methods that produce labels from several protocols at once have so far been restricted to fixed, explicitly provided hierarchies of protocols, trained on limited domains or specialized to natural images. Stochastic segmentation methods, built on variational autoencoders, diffusion models, Gaussian models or in-context stochastic models, capture ambiguity and rater variability, but within a single pre-specified task rather than across different plausible protocols for a task never seen during training.

This raises the following problem: given a collection of images from a previously unseen biomedical domain, without any manual annotations, example segmentations or user prompts, and without prior knowledge of the number of labels or their shapes, can one automatically produce several complete, multi-label segmentation maps corresponding to different plausible protocols, such that within each protocol a given label denotes the same structure in every image of the collection? Such a capability would let a researcher or clinician choose, among the proposed protocols, the one that best fits their downstream use. The problem is challenging because the space of plausible protocols is large and ambiguous, the outputs must be both diverse across protocols and coherent across images, available training data usually provide only one protocol and often only one labelled structure per dataset.

taches.questions:
The success of large language models (LLMs) has spurred the development of vision-language models (VLMs) capable of processing and generating content from both visual and textual inputs. Recent VLMs demonstrate impressive performance in tasks including image captioning, visual question answering, and multimodal dialogue. However, as VLMs increase in scale and complexity, their inference times grow substantially, posing significant challenges for practical deployment. The computational cost of processing high-dimensional image inputs, coupled with the autoregressive nature of text generation, results in significant inference latency, and inference efficiency remains a critical bottleneck.

Speculative decoding has proven effective in accelerating LLM inference by employing a smaller, faster draft model to propose candidate token sequences, which the larger target model verifies in parallel. Correct predictions from the draft model let the target model skip costly autoregressive computations, yielding speedups of 3-4x on text-only tasks while provably preserving the target model's output distribution. Many refinements exist for text: self-speculative drafting, multiple decoding heads attached to the target model, drafters that consume the target model's hidden states, draft trees, and multi-token prediction. Since a VLM keeps the LLM architecture unchanged and merely inserts visual embeddings into the input sequence, these methods can in principle be applied directly to VLMs by treating visual embeddings as part of the context.

In practice, however, speculative decoding for VLMs remains underexplored, and prior attempts achieve only marginal speedups (below 1.5x). The only notable prior effort applied speculative decoding to a 7B VLM with a small language-only draft model and reached at most 1.5x; a small VLM draft model incorporating an image encoder yielded only marginal gains. A plausible cause is a fundamental difference between textual and visual data: text is abstract and information-dense, whereas images, despite their visual richness, often contain considerable redundancy. Large VLMs may be able to filter redundant image information layer by layer without compromising textual comprehension, whereas small, shallow draft models struggle to extract pertinent visual information from long, redundant sequences of image embeddings while preserving textual coherence. As generated responses grow long, visual tokens also become buried in the middle of the context, where shallow models are known to attend poorly. A further obstacle is the scarcity of large-scale, publicly available multimodal datasets with extended assistant responses, which are needed to train a draft model that imitates the target VLM over long generations.

The open problem is therefore: how can a lightweight draft model be made to use visual context effectively enough that speculative decoding delivers substantial, lossless acceleration for VLMs across different model families and diverse multimodal tasks, and how can such a draft model be trained given the lack of suitable long-response multimodal data?

taches.questions:
The generalization behavior of overparameterized neural networks presents fundamental challenges to classical statistical learning theory. Traditional complexity measures, such as parameter counts or spectral norms of weights, form the basis of many generalization bounds, including those derived from VC dimension theory and Rademacher complexity. However, these approaches do not adequately explain several empirical phenomena, e.g., double descent and benign overfitting. The occurrence of double descent illustrates that the test error, after initially increasing near the interpolation threshold, can improve as the model size continues to grow. Similarly, the phenomenon of benign overfitting demonstrates that models that perfectly interpolate noisy training data can nonetheless achieve strong generalization. Such findings expose the limitations of norm- and size-based complexity measures as predictors of generalization.

A large-scale empirical study evaluating more than forty complexity measures found that many norm-based quantities not only fail to correlate with generalization, but often even correlate negatively. Beyond optimization-related metrics, one of the few quantities that consistently correlated with generalization was the margin, i.e., the distance to the decision boundary. This aligns with an emerging perspective: generalization in modern networks is governed less by model size or norms, and more by the stability or robustness of predictions under input perturbations. Related insights also arise from the literature on algorithmic stability and flat minima. However, most theoretical results in this direction are restricted to linear models.

An exception is the universal law of robustness from prior work, which, under mild distributional assumptions, establishes a formal link between robustness, generalization, and overparameterization: smoothness and overparameterization need to balance in order to ensure good generalization while overfitting. This law relies on the assumption that the function class is Lipschitz, which makes it inadequate for classifiers whose codomain is discrete by design. Its originators leave open the challenge "to understand for which notions of smoothness there is a tradeoff with size." Simply focusing on the Lipschitz constant of an underlying score function g, where the classifier is of the form f = argmax ∘ g, does not resolve this: since g can be arbitrarily rescaled without changing the predictions of f, its Lipschitz constant need not reflect the geometry of the decision boundary.

This raises several questions. Which geometric notion of robustness is meaningful for discontinuous classifiers, and can it control the capacity of a hypothesis class to fit random labels, so that generalization guarantees improve as robustness increases? Does a law of robustness hold for classification, i.e., must classifiers that nearly interpolate their training data be non-robust unless they are substantially overparameterized, and at what scale of parameterization relative to sample size and input dimension? Can such statements be extended from finite hypothesis classes to infinite, parameterized function classes such as neural networks? And empirically, how does the robustness of near-interpolating networks change with model size, does it track test performance, and how does it compare with traditional norm-based measures in this respect?

taches.questions:
Image fusion aims to merge images from different modalities into a single fused image that contains the complementary information of each. It has wide applications: infrared and visible image fusion enhances perception under adverse conditions by combining the detailed information of visible images with the thermal radiation characteristics of infrared images; medical image fusion mitigates the information discrepancies between MRI and CT modalities to provide more comprehensive diagnostic support; and multi-exposure and multi-focus image fusion merge images taken with different exposures or focal planes to synthesize high-quality photographs.

Since the advent of Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models, diffusion-based methods have been widely adopted across computer vision, including image fusion. Compared to traditional fusion approaches, diffusion-based methods not only integrate information from multiple source images effectively but also enhance the visual quality of the fused results. Benefiting from the powerful priors encoded in pre-trained diffusion models, they show great potential in multi-task fusion scenarios, where a single unified framework can be adapted to various fusion tasks. Prior approaches of this kind introduce fusion priors into the sampling process of a pre-trained diffusion model through posterior sampling, effectively improving fusion quality.

However, the long inference times of these methods pose significant challenges for real-world applications. They typically require hundreds of sampling steps to achieve satisfactory results, and reducing the number of steps to improve efficiency often leads to a substantial drop in fusion performance. Strategies for accelerating diffusion models, such as distillation and latent-space diffusion, have been widely explored, but their application to image fusion remains limited. Existing distillation methods can enable single-step sampling but usually require fine-tuning tailored to specific model architectures and datasets, lacking generalization across diverse fusion tasks. Latent-space diffusion based on Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) can significantly reduce computational cost, but the autoencoder's training objective primarily targets image reconstruction rather than image fusion. Reconstruction focuses on pixel-level fidelity to the original input, whereas fusion must capture complementary semantic information across modalities and decode an image that integrates several inputs and differs from each of them; this discrepancy makes the direct use of reconstruction-trained autoencoders in fusion challenging.

The problem is therefore how to accelerate diffusion-based image fusion, ideally down to very few or a single sampling step, while preserving fusion quality and keeping the ability of one model to generalize across different fusion tasks. A related question is how latent-space representations can be made suitable for fusion despite the mismatch between reconstruction-oriented autoencoder objectives and the requirements of image fusion.

taches.questions:
Ordering-based causal discovery aims to identify a topological ordering of the nodes of a causal graph, typically a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), such that the order reflects the underlying cause-effect relationships. Combinatorial search over DAG structures is NP-hard, with complexity increasing sharply as the number of variables grows. Ordering-based approaches instead first infer a topological order and then determine the direction of edges from this order, which substantially reduces the number of candidate graph structures. When Large Language Models (LLMs) are used, predicting causal orderings rather than full graph structures has been reported to improve consistency and reduce structural errors, and a causal order alone suffices to identify valid backdoor adjustment sets without full graph discovery.

Under the Additive Noise Model (ANM) assumption, several causal ordering methods based on score matching (SCORE, CaPS and DiffAN) determine the causal order by iteratively identifying and removing leaf nodes, i.e., variables that do not influence any others in the causal graph. To do so, they require the Jacobian of the score function $\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{x})=\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\log P(\mathbf{x})$, in particular its diagonal, the Hessian diagonal of the log-density, whose variance or mean is examined after each leaf removal to select the next leaf. The accuracy of this estimate is therefore central, and existing estimators have important weaknesses. SCORE and CaPS rely on the second-order Stein gradient estimator; such kernel-based estimators exhibit cubic computational complexity with respect to the number of samples, suffer from numerical instability due to kernel matrix inversion, and must be re-estimated at every ordering step, which becomes computationally and memory-wise problematic for large causal graphs, since causal discovery requires more samples as the number of nodes grows. DiffAN instead learns the score with a denoising diffusion model and, rather than retraining, approximates the scores of the remaining variables after leaf removal through second-order derivatives of the initially trained score model. This reduces the computational burden and scales with the number of samples, but its performance degrades in high-dimensional settings: conventional MLP score models frequently struggle to estimate derivatives accurately, so the curvature information of the learned model can deviate from that of the true score function, and computing second-order derivatives of score models is numerically unstable. Because leaves are identified sequentially, errors in these derivative estimates may accumulate throughout the ordering process and ultimately degrade causal discovery performance.

A first question is therefore how to obtain a stable and accurate approximation of the Hessian diagonal of the log-density, including reliable second-order derivatives of a learned score model, that remains memory-efficient and scalable as the number of variables and samples grows, and that can improve existing score-matching-based ordering algorithms under both linear and nonlinear additive noise models.

A second question concerns semantic information. Recent studies leverage the prior knowledge of LLMs to improve causal reasoning, but these approaches often treat LLM responses as binary decisions, failing to reflect the uncertainty in that prior knowledge, and they remain structurally incompatible with ordering-based approaches that sequentially predict leaf nodes. In addition, pairwise prompting methods require a number of LLM queries that grows quadratically with the number of variables, and in many domains variable names are abstracted and metadata are scarce or uncertain. How can statistics estimated from observational data be combined in a principled, probabilistic way with the priors of autoregressive generative models such as LLMs, so as to obtain more reliable causal orderings, ideally without fine-tuning or intensive prompt engineering?

taches.questions:
Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations are indispensable ingredients in chemistry, materials, drug discovery, and other fields. Given the molecular system of interest within a particular chemical environment, the essence of MD is to obtain the conformational ensemble that follows laws of physics through in silico simulation, which provides accurate estimates of kinetic (e.g., dissociation rate constant) and thermodynamic (e.g., free energy) observables. Under certain conditions, the equilibrium measure of molecular ensembles follows the Boltzmann distribution. To obtain such equilibrium samples in practice, classical MD simulations widely rely on Langevin dynamics, which models the temporal evolution of the system through a Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) and induces a Markov-chain sampling process whose stationary distribution corresponds to the Boltzmann distribution. Although these methods have been firmly established in practice, the stability of numerical integration requires exceedingly small time steps (around 1 femtosecond), making the computational cost prohibitively high for long-timescale or high-throughput simulations.

Recently, the rise of deep learning methods has opened up new possibilities for boosting MD simulations and ensemble generation. One line of work replaces empirical force fields with accurate all-atom neural network potentials in order to accelerate simulations of large biomolecular systems; this approach, however, does not overcome the inherent limitations of sequential trajectory generation with small time steps. Another line of work leverages generative models to fit the empirical distribution from MD trajectories, while Boltzmann generators further reproduce the Boltzmann distribution from a surrogate model by importance sampling. Such methods enable highly efficient parallel generation of independent and identically distributed samples, yet the absence of temporal dependencies blocks further estimation of kinetic observables.

A third paradigm, time-coarsened dynamics, seeks to fit the conditional distribution mu(x_{t+tau} | x_t), defined as the transition density of the underlying MD process that maps a current state x_t to its distribution after a lag tau much larger than the integration step, thereby enabling time-dependent trajectory generation on a coarse-grained temporal scale. This paradigm achieves substantial efficiency gains while preserving both the kinetic and thermodynamic properties of the system. However, several challenges remain in the literature. First, the stability of trajectory generation over long timescales cannot yet be reliably ensured, since generation from an initial state is prone to error accumulation and even minor deviations may push a model out of distribution. In addition, most existing methods are confined to one specific molecular domain (e.g., proteins) and therefore fail to model cross-domain systems. Prior work has used 3D molecular pretraining to obtain a unified atomic representation model, demonstrating strong generalization for cross-domain MD simulations; however, the inconsistency between pretraining on single structures and finetuning on trajectory pairs could result in suboptimal transfer and hinder the effective use of pretrained knowledge. A further limitation of most existing methods is their focus on single-molecule simulations, while multi-molecular systems such as protein-ligand complexes have been much less explored.

Two further difficulties frame the problem. Progress is hard to achieve by training solely on MD data, because accurate MD trajectories are expensive to generate and data produced by empirical force fields have poor accuracy and adaptability across diverse molecular domains, which also limits the molecular diversity of available trajectory data. And for protein-ligand systems, the task of interest is to locate the global minimum-energy conformation rather than to reconstruct the full Boltzmann distribution, yet protein-ligand interaction can occur on the millisecond timescale or longer, making its simulation computationally prohibitive even for models operating at coarsened timesteps; generating trajectories directly from the unbound state to the bound state therefore remains out of reach.

The resulting question is how to learn time-coarsened biomolecular dynamics that generalizes across molecular domains, that remains stable and physically plausible over long generated trajectories, that exploits the structural information held in large databases of single high-resolution structures despite the limited molecular diversity of trajectory data, and that reaches the relevant bound conformations of multi-molecular systems within short generated trajectories, while still reproducing the thermodynamic and kinetic observables that classical MD provides.

taches.questions:
Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have significantly improved their performance across a broad range of Visual Question Answering (VQA) tasks. Traditional VQA benchmarks primarily evaluate whether models can provide correct answers to clearly stated, unambiguous questions paired with well-defined images. While such benchmarks are valuable for assessing basic multimodal reasoning, they fail to capture a critical challenge in real-world use: the ability to handle ambiguous or unclear queries. This capability remains underexplored.

In human communication, ambiguity is typically resolved through contextual inference or follow-up questions. For example, when asked "What brand is this vehicle?" about an image with multiple cars, one may seek clarification or infer the intended car from context. Previous research in ambiguous VQA has mainly focused on making models always ask clarifying questions when uncertain. While this binary answer-or-ask strategy can be useful, it does not reflect real-world conversational dynamics, where clarification is not always the most efficient approach. Humans instead adapt their strategy to the situation: sometimes inferring intent from context, sometimes offering multiple plausible answers when they are few, and requesting clarification only when necessary.

Ambiguity has been extensively studied in text-based question answering, whereas visual question answering research has only recently begun to address it. Prior analyses show that VLMs often produce answers to ambiguous questions that appear plausible but lack semantic adequacy, and existing efforts either evaluate how visual context helps resolve ambiguous expressions or train models to always seek clarification, without adapting to different types or degrees of ambiguity. More broadly, LLMs and VLMs tend to answer even unanswerable questions, and earlier remedies have been binary: answer when confident, abstain when uncertain. Yet simply abstaining does not align with how humans behave, who may leverage contextual clues to infer the answer, enumerate the possibilities when only a few are viable, or ask a follow-up question.

This leaves open several questions. How should the different kinds and degrees of ambiguity in visual questions be systematically categorized, and what response strategy is most appropriate for each? Do current open-source and proprietary VLMs adapt their response strategy to the ambiguity they face?And can VLMs be made to recognize ambiguity and autonomously select a context-appropriate strategy, such as answering directly, inferring intent from context, listing plausible alternatives, or requesting clarification, while remaining faithful to the image content?

taches.questions:
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in natural language understanding, reasoning, and generation, and their potential for scientific applications has recently attracted increasing attention. Scientific data, however, is often multimodal, and time series represents one of the most fundamental and widely encountered modalities across disciplines such as physics, astronomy, biology, and engineering. Understanding and generating scientific time series is critical for analysing diverse signals, such as astronomical light curves, neural recordings, and bioacoustic vocalisations, as well as for tasks such as stellar collision detection and forecasting physiological states. However, scientific time series remain largely under-explored for LLMs. Bridging this gap is pivotal to transforming LLMs from narrative assistants into engines that can interrogate dynamical systems, drive scientific discovery, and guide experimental design.

Current multimodal LLMs typically handle time series by either directly encoding numerical sequences as text or converting signals into images. Representing time series as text can lead to very long sequences that LLMs may struggle to process, while image-based representations may sacrifice numerical precision. These approaches may therefore fail to capture the rich temporal dynamics, long-range dependencies, and domain-specific patterns inherent in scientific time series, limiting a model's ability to perform both comprehensive analysis and accurate generation. On the other hand, models specifically designed for time series have traditionally been developed for individual tasks, domains, or datasets, which limits their applicability beyond narrow settings. Unifying time series modelling across diverse domains is non-trivial, since signals exhibit varying scales, sampling frequencies, dimensions, lengths, and dynamic patterns. Existing unified time series models make progress toward cross-domain applicability but typically focus on specific task types, such as forecasting or analytical tasks, and their effectiveness on non-periodic, heterogeneous scientific signals remains unclear. Moreover, these models often rely on specialised architecture designs that are not readily incorporated into LLMs.

The role of LLMs in time series modelling is itself debated: LLM-based forecasters have been reported to perform no better than strong non-LLM baselines, highlighting the difficulty of transferring linguistic pretraining to temporal prediction. Multimodal approaches that treat time series as an additional modality, and alignment-based methods that adapt temporal signals into language-compatible forms, have been proposed, but existing approaches largely focus on either understanding or generation rather than a unified treatment of both, and approaches that integrate question answering and forecasting tend to rely on separate architectures that are not compatible with general-purpose LLM training. On the evaluation side, time series benchmarks have mostly targeted forecasting, anomaly detection, and question answering in domains such as finance, weather, and traffic, while scientific domains such as astronomy and earth science have not been extensively studied; current scientific benchmarks for LLMs focus on reasoning over text and images, which loses information when temporal data is converted into visual formats.

This raises several open questions. How well do current text-only LLMs, multimodal LLMs, and specialised time series models actually handle scientific time series that span many disciplines, both understanding and generation tasks, univariate and multivariate signals, and widely varying lengths and sampling frequencies? Are general-purpose LLMs or specialised time series models better able to generalise to scientific domains they have rarely seen, and are text or image representations of signals adequate for such tasks? What ingredients are necessary to extend general-purpose LLMs so that they can both understand and generate heterogeneous scientific time series while remaining compatible with general-purpose LLM training, and can the shortcomings of existing models be overcome simply by finetuning them, or do they stem from their architecture?

taches.questions:
Over the past few years, considerable effort has been devoted to developing unified models capable of both multimodal understanding and generation. Many such models, e.g., Show-o and MetaQuery, have achieved impressive results on text-to-image generation, yet this paradigm falters when extended to instruction-guided image editing. Even recent integrative and connector-based methods such as BAGEL, UniWorld-V1, and Step1X-Edit show a substantial performance gap with proprietary models like GPT-4o-Image on mainstream image editing benchmarks, even when built on large understanding and generation backbones such as Qwen2.5-VL-7B and FLUX.1-dev. Much current research focuses on scaling parameters and data or on architectural modifications, but it is unclear that scale alone addresses the underlying difficulty.

In current image editing models, user instructions are typically translated into semantic conditions by a semantic encoder, usually a multimodal large language model, and this process lacks intermediate reasoning or refinement. The resulting conditions are forwarded to the generation module, which must then simultaneously organize the layout of the edited image, recognize existing objects, localize the edit area, render new content, and preserve unchanged regions. The understanding module thus functions merely as a translator, while the generation module is burdened with both design and painting. This division of responsibilities is counterintuitive: the understanding module is typically trained with several times more data on complex reasoning tasks than the generation module, and in natural human workflows, planning and refinement precede the act of drawing.

The available training data compounds the problem. Prompts in existing text-to-image datasets are typically short and simple; while they capture the semantics of the target image, they do little to foster the long-context comprehension that complex instruction following requires. In image editing datasets the issue is even more pronounced: instructions often consist of only a few descriptive words and may fail to reflect the actual change between source and target images, either because AI editors over-edit (for instance removing objects not mentioned in the prompt) or because human operators misunderstand or misapply edits. Even when a prompt correctly describes the intended change, an overly simple instruction such as "change the background" can admit multiple equally valid edits.

These observations raise several questions. How should responsibilities be divided between the understanding and generation modules of a unified model for image editing? Can a more balanced division, rather than greater model scale, substantially improve the precision of instruction-guided edits and close the gap with proprietary editors, even for compact models? And what kind of training data would allow a model to exploit such a division?

domains: degeneration detection in long-form text generation

taches.questions:
Recent large language models (LLMs) display sophisticated capabilities such as mathematical reasoning and planning, suggesting that they internally process information through complex, nonlinear and potentially hierarchical mechanisms, even though they operate through simple token-by-token predictions. How such macroscopic behaviors emerge from microscopic predictive steps remains an important open question, essential for understanding both the potential and the limitations of these models. Although minimizing next-token prediction loss (perplexity) is theoretically powerful, it falls short of explaining unexpected model behaviors such as hallucinations and repetitive, bland or incoherent outputs, which can occur even when perplexity is low. New tools for characterizing the complex behavior of LLMs are therefore needed.

Current evaluation approaches broadly fall into two categories. The first relies on local textual properties, such as lexical or syntactic statistics (e.g., n-gram frequencies); these metrics are intuitive and interpretable but often fail to capture semantic ambiguities or deeper structural complexity. The second consists of global metrics, such as mean perplexity or semantic similarity measures; these provide comprehensive quantitative evaluations but often lack interpretability and a connection to underlying local textual properties. This divide between local interpretability and global comprehensiveness reflects a broader challenge: bridging the microscopic (token-level) and macroscopic (long-range, structural) perspectives on LLM behavior.

A related line of work studies statistical self-similarity in language, i.e., approximate scale invariance identified statistically in empirical data. Such self-similarity has been documented through Zipf's law for word frequencies, Herdan-Heaps' law for vocabulary growth, and long-range correlations in word occurrences across text spans. Some studies have looked for fractal structure at the semantic level, for instance in latent semantic analysis embeddings of paragraphs or in word vectors, but these rely on static representations that do not vary with context and therefore have limited utility for characterizing language models. Other work has compared scale-free properties of generated and natural texts, proposed statistical tests for such deviations under different sampling strategies, studied mutual-information scaling for long-context modeling, or measured scaling exponents of cumulative log-perplexity series and related them to downstream performance; the latter, however, primarily captures long-range dependencies in the model's prediction-error sequence rather than the structure of the generated language itself. Self-similarity of texts as seen through autoregressive LLMs has also been reported across languages, but the linguistic significance of this self-similarity and the explicit role of the language model in capturing it remain unexplored.

A closely related practical problem is degeneration in long-text generation: texts that become repetitive, incoherent or bland. Explicit repetition is easy to detect, but subtler forms of degeneration such as incoherence and blandness lack clear definitions and reliable quantification methods, and existing metrics each capture only some of these failure modes.

This raises several research questions. Can one define a measure, computable from what an autoregressive language model already produces at inference time, that connects local properties of text with its global, long-range structural complexity? Since real language models are imperfect, and small errors on rare outcomes barely affect the training loss, is such a measure still meaningful and stable as a description of the complexity of a text as perceived by a model? How does it relate to the intrinsic complexity of a text, to the amount of context available to the model, and to the progress of pre-training, beyond what perplexity shows? Can it reveal model behaviors that perplexity misses, such as a tendency to hallucinate on knowledge-intensive text, and can it serve as a single, intrinsic indicator of the different forms of degeneration in generated text? Finally, for such a measure to be useful in practice, it should be cheap enough to compute alongside standard inference and broadly applicable across models.

taches.questions:
Diffusion models have proven effective for a wide range of generation tasks, including text-to-image, audio and video generation. In image generation, a neural network is trained to progressively denoise images corrupted by Gaussian noise, and at test time a sampling process starts from random noise and applies the network repeatedly to recover a clean image. Producing realistic images typically requires many denoising steps, which makes sampling computationally demanding. One line of work reduces the number of denoising steps; another compresses the network itself, for example through quantization or pruning, to lower the cost of each step.

Network quantization maps full-precision weights and activations to lower bit-widths, enabling fixed-point computation for efficient inference. Quantization-aware training optimizes network weights and quantization parameters (such as step sizes and zero-points) jointly on the full training set, which is computationally expensive and hard to apply to large models. Post-training quantization instead calibrates only the quantization parameters, without retraining the weights, using a small subset of samples, and has therefore attracted considerable attention.

Post-training quantization methods were, however, designed mainly for discriminative networks such as image classifiers, and applying them directly to diffusion models is challenging because sampling is a sequential process. As sampling proceeds, the quantization error introduced at each denoising step propagates to the following steps. The overall error at a given step can thus be split into two parts: the quantization error made at the current step, and the error accumulated along all previous steps. Most existing methods for quantizing diffusion models neglect the accumulated part: they feed the same error-free input to both the full-precision and the quantized model at every step and calibrate quantization parameters to minimize the difference between their outputs step by step, ignoring that, during actual sampling, the input of the quantized model carries errors accumulated over earlier steps. Recent attempts to address accumulated errors either handle only single-step errors or rely on additional per-step parameters for error correction, which add memory and computational overhead at sampling time.

This raises the following questions. How much does error accumulation across denoising steps, as opposed to per-step error, contribute to the degradation of quantized diffusion models? How can the quantization parameters of a diffusion model be calibrated post-training so that the overall quantization error, including the part accumulated over previous denoising steps, is reduced, rather than only the error of each step taken in isolation? And how can such calibration be made efficient enough, in memory and computation, to scale to large diffusion models, without introducing extra parameters or extra cost during sampling, while keeping the quantized model's outputs close to those of its full-precision counterpart, especially at low bit-widths?

taches.questions:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have catalyzed a shift from isolated model capabilities towards collaborative multi-agent systems. Frameworks such as CAMEL, AutoGen, and ChatDev have demonstrated that LLMs can collaborate effectively, leveraging the strengths of individual models to solve complex problems that are beyond the capabilities of a single model.

While multi-agent systems have shown great promise, they also introduce new challenges, particularly in inter-agent communication, which is crucial for their success. Explicit communication through natural language has been explored to let models share information, coordinate their actions, and make collective decisions. However, natural language communication incurs high inference costs due to the need for multiple decoding steps, and it may not fully capture the rich information that needs to be shared, as information is lost in the sampling process that occurs as each new token is produced.

To address this limitation, recent works have explored communication protocols that leverage the internal representations of LLMs. CIPHER uses the embedding space as the medium of communication, passing the weighted average of the token embeddings from one LLM to another. AC instead transmits intermediate activations, specifically the last token's hidden state, replacing the last token's hidden state of the receiver model with that of the sender model (or averaging the two). While these methods are promising, they still face challenges in communication efficiency and effectiveness: CIPHER still requires multiple decoding steps, which can be costly, and AC may lose information since only limited activation information is transmitted and the receiver's own state is overwritten.

Formally, consider solving a contextual task through the communication of two LLMs: a sender, which takes as input a context and produces the information to be communicated, and a receiver, which takes as input a query together with the information from the sender and produces the final output. The two LLMs may be two instances of the same LLM, or two models fine-tuned from the same base LLM. The objective is to design a communication protocol that jointly optimizes communication cost, computation efficiency, and the fidelity of the information passed from sender to receiver.

This raises the question: what is the most effective way to communicate between LLMs? An ideal protocol should satisfy three criteria. Effectiveness: the receiver should be able to effectively utilize the information from the sender. Efficiency: the protocol should minimize the computation needed by the sender and the amount of data transmitted between models. Generality: it should apply to a wide range of tasks and model architectures. An open question is which kind of internal information is best suited as a communication medium.

taches.questions:
End-to-end autonomous driving has emerged as a promising paradigm that jointly learns perception, prediction, and planning in a unified framework. Compared to traditional modular pipelines, this approach simplifies system design and enables planning-oriented optimization through holistic training. Recent advances have demonstrated that directly generating future trajectories from raw sensor inputs can achieve strong performance, highlighting the potential of end-to-end methods for building scalable and efficient driving systems. Such methods have been evaluated in both open-loop and closed-loop settings, across real-world datasets and simulation platforms.

Despite these successes, most existing methods adopt a one-shot paradigm, in which sensor observations, typically from the current time step, are used to directly predict a trajectory several seconds into the future. In this setup, the model must rely heavily on the scene's current situation to infer the ego vehicle's future motion. While effective in structured environments, this tends to underestimate the importance of how the scene may evolve over time, a crucial factor in dynamic and interactive driving contexts. Furthermore, the ego vehicle's own future actions can significantly influence how the surrounding scene unfolds. These two aspects, the future scene and the agent's future behavior, are inherently coupled, yet this bidirectional dependency remains underexplored in current end-to-end systems.

In a parallel line of work, world models aim to predict future scene dynamics conditioned on the current environment and ego state, either by generating realistic future videos or by generating structured scene representations. Some works have begun to connect world modeling with planning: some extend a world model with action tokens to jointly generate future scene states and ego actions, while others start from an end-to-end driving pipeline and use world modeling either as an additional supervision signal during training or to help select the best trajectory among multiple candidates. In these designs, the anticipated future scene and the planned trajectory influence each other only weakly.

The problem is therefore how an end-to-end driving system can take into account, when planning, how the scene is likely to evolve, and conversely how its own intended actions shape that evolution, so that scene anticipation and trajectory planning inform each other, while remaining efficient enough for driving and improving planning quality in complex, dynamic scenarios over one-shot planners.

taches.questions:
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance across a broad spectrum of tasks. However, as LLMs grow in size, so does their computational burden, making them difficult to deploy in resource-constrained environments such as mobile phones, edge devices and embedded systems. The challenge is to make large models more efficient and accessible without sacrificing performance. Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful technique for model compression, enabling smaller student models to mimic a larger teacher model; for LLMs it plays a central role in transferring capabilities such as natural language understanding, reasoning and instruction following onto smaller models. Early distillation approaches transfer soft labels via output logits, while subsequent work explores richer supervision signals such as the alignment of intermediate features.

Although LLMs are trained for a broad range of tasks, one often wants a smaller, task-specific model when full task coverage is not required, particularly in resource-constrained environments. Task-aware knowledge distillation has been proposed to selectively transfer task-relevant knowledge from teacher to student. These methods, however, typically assume access to large datasets, whereas in many real-world applications the amount of available data is limited and high-quality human-annotated data is expensive to obtain. Despite algorithmic advances in task-aware distillation for LLMs, the problem of selecting the data used for distillation has received limited interest, particularly in few-shot settings, where the student must be distilled from the teacher using only a very small number of samples labeled for the task (shots). Earlier studies of distillation under low-data regimes in classical machine learning do not address the challenges specific to distilling LLMs, so few-shot task-aware distillation remains underexplored for LLMs.

The setting is difficult: in classical machine learning, few-shot training generalizes poorly and causes ineffective distillation because a handful of samples gives insufficient coverage of the task. At the same time, few-shot distillation holds potential for LLMs, because they are pretrained on large corpora and few-shot learning has been successful with such models.

This raises the following questions. Given a teacher model trained for a classification task and a budget of only k labeled examples, how can a much smaller student model be distilled so that it faithfully reproduces the teacher's task behavior and decision-making? Which examples carry the most information about the teacher's decisions when data is extremely scarce, and can the composition of the small distillation set be improved without collecting more human-labeled data?

taches.questions:
The fitness landscape is a nearly century-old foundational concept rooted in evolutionary biology, with profound implications on the understanding of biological principles in all 3 modalities of the central dogma (DNA, RNA, protein) - from drug resistance, enzyme activity, protein stability and expression, RNA folding and function, to transcription factor binding. Efficiently and accurately mapping these fitness landscape surfaces is critical to enable various downstream tasks, and has been recently advanced by machine learning (ML) models that can capture complex and high-dimensional patterns of the sequence-fitness map.

A critical step in developing these models is their proper performance evaluation to understand limitations and enable comparisons with existing methods. For this purpose, large-scale benchmarks have been established across different modalities. For example, ProteinGym offers more than 250 tasks curated from deep mutational scanning (DMS) assays for proteins, while RNAGym incorporates over 30 standardized RNA DMS assays. Considering their impressive scales and the famous "no free lunch" theorem, it is often unrealistic to expect one single model to dominate on all tasks. For instance, the model that yields the highest average score across all 217 DMS substitution tasks in ProteinGym leads in only 14 (6.5%) individual tasks, while 44 out of the 89 evaluated models lead in at least one task. This reality prompts critical questions: Q1: "Why did one model perform well on one set of tasks but poorly on another?"; Q2: "Why did one model outperform baseline on one task, but not on the other?"

Answering these questions necessitates informative features that characterize each task. Unfortunately, existing benchmarks typically provide only basic labels (e.g., taxon) or statistics (e.g., sequence length), which are insufficient to fully elucidate the 2 questions above. Consequently, users often rely on average scores for decision-making and comparison, which can lead to biased conclusions. Even grouping scores based on basic task features (e.g., mutational type, taxon) or analyzing the performance distribution, though it can offer additional information, is not sufficient to fully address these 2 questions, so benchmarks of this scale have not yet been fully leveraged.

For decades, evolutionary biologists have developed various features to quantitatively characterize topographical aspects of fitness landscapes, including ruggedness, navigability, epistasis, and neutrality. The most intuitive and widely studied aspect is ruggedness, often characterized by the presence of multiple local optima; a necessary condition for it is epistasis, which occurs when one or more mutations interact, whereas a purely additive landscape, where mutational effects are independent, would be fairly smooth with a single global optimum. Ruggedness along with pervasive epistasis can pose a fundamental challenge to an evolving population's ability to find the highest peak, thus reducing the landscape's navigability, while neutrality describes the presence of "plateaus" consisting of genotypes sharing the same fitness. Such features have been extensively applied to unveil fundamental principles governing evolutionary dynamics.

Yet, despite decades of study, landscape analysis remains a highly specialized biological field. As a result, standard open-source implementations for calculating many landscape features are rarely available. Also, existing research often targets specific landscape aspects, leaving no consensus on a comprehensive feature set. In addition, empirical landscapes span diverse biological modalities and scales, further complicating the development of unified analysis tools. The rapid growth in empirical data also demands highly scalable methods, since mutagenesis libraries can now reach millions of variants, and real-world empirical landscapes often suffer from missing variants, experimental noise in fitness measurement, or biased sampling of the mutant library. The few existing landscape analysis packages offer several quantitative metrics but are limited in scope, handle landscapes only up to the scale of about 100,000 variants, and, being written in C, hinder interoperability with modern ML ecosystems. Consequently, researchers currently lack accessible, broadly applicable tools for characterizing fitness landscape features in common benchmarking tasks.

taches.questions:
The ability to process long contexts is crucial for Large Language Models (LLMs). However, processing such long contexts poses significant challenges: pre-trained LLMs face both architectural and computational constraints in handling extended contexts. In particular, as the context length increases, the complexity of attention mechanisms increases quadratically (O(n^2)), while the storage overhead of the key-value (KV) cache increases linearly (O(n)).

Various approaches have been proposed to address this challenge, with KV cache compression emerging as a promising direction. These methods aim to compress the KV cache while preserving the information needed to maintain model performance. A straightforward strategy is to keep tokens with high historical importance, for example as measured by accumulated attention scores, leveraging the observation that attention weights vary significantly across tokens. Other work tries to identify more general notions of token importance, such as keeping initial and recent tokens, or using norms or entropy. However, these approaches share a fundamental limitation: by discarding tokens outright, they fail to retain tokens that are unimportant in the history but suddenly become critical for subsequent predictions.

To reduce the information loss caused by hard pruning, cache merging methods have been proposed that merge multiple cache positions into fewer representations, thereby preserving more information. These merging approaches implicitly assume that certain redundancies or patterns exist in the KV cache, and they typically apply the same merging operation to the keys and the values. This raises a fundamental question that has not been examined: what specific characteristics of LLM attention lead to these redundancies and make cache merging feasible? In particular, do keys and values stored in the cache exhibit the same kind of local redundancy, and is it justified to merge them in the same way? Answering this question matters for designing compression schemes that reduce the memory and compute cost of long-context inference while losing as little of the information needed for later predictions as possible.

taches.questions:
With the advancement of text-to-image generative models, there has been growing interest in controllable image generation. A recent line of work generates images conditioned on layouts, commonly referred to as Layout-to-Image (L2I) generation, which allows users to directly specify the spatial locations and counts of objects in the generated outputs. Prior L2I methods have mostly fine-tuned foundational text-to-image models to inject layout conditioning, either in U-Net backbones (through inserted layers or manipulated attention maps and masks) or, more recently, in diffusion Transformer architectures such as Flux or SD3; in parallel, training-free approaches use guidance mechanisms inside diffusion models to enforce spatial constraints, often treating the layout only as a soft constraint.

While existing frameworks can achieve satisfactory spatial and numerical control, they fail to generate distinct, coherent objects when multiple bounding boxes overlap in the layout and their associated categories are semantically similar. Such scenarios lead to artifacts including object blending, spatial ambiguity and visual distortion. Two factors appear to be involved: the extent of the spatial overlap between boxes, and how little semantic distinction there is between the overlapping instances. How much each factor contributes to degraded generation, and how to measure the difficulty that a given layout poses for an L2I model, remain open questions.

Evaluation is a second obstacle. The most widely used benchmark for L2I generation, COCO, provides entity bounding boxes with simple category labels but lacks detailed image-level and instance-level captions, which limits its utility for semantically rich generation. More recent layout benchmarks, such as HiCo-7k (7,000 samples curated from GriT-20M) and LayoutSAM (5,000 samples selected from SAM-1B), add detailed annotations but rely on GroundingDINO for bounding box extraction, a detector known for limited recognition performance and frequent false positives; HiCo-7k partially addresses this through manual curation, whereas LayoutSAM has no human intervention. These benchmarks primarily focus on image quality and offer limited evaluation of complex layouts or of the accuracy of generated relationships between instances. Whether they contain enough densely overlapping, semantically entangled layouts to assess models under these challenging, realistic conditions is unclear.

The problem is therefore threefold: how to quantify the difficulty that overlapping, semantically similar bounding boxes pose for layout-to-image generation; how to evaluate L2I models reliably across the full range of such difficulty, including the fidelity of overlapping regions and of the relationships between instances; and how L2I models could be made to generate distinct, coherent objects when their bounding boxes overlap heavily.
